## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

*Physical AI stack focus for this chapter.*

_Why can a machine pass its normal operating tests and still fail when its protective response is needed?_

The claims that matter most in a physical machine describe what it does after something has already gone wrong, when the learned proposer stalls, an observation arrives old, a message is lost, or the supply sags while a loaded body moves toward a person. Normal operation almost never exercises those responses, so thousands of clean runs can coexist with a stopping mechanism that has never once been made to stop the machine. Without deliberate testing, the first real trial of that mechanism happens in service, where a late response delivers energy that no software correction can recall. Establishing such a claim requires creating the fault on purpose, measuring the physical response with instruments the fault cannot reach, and scoring it against acceptance conditions fixed before the test, and every condition left untested still limits what the result can support. Verification makes those limits explicit before release grants any action authority to cross the causal boundary.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Derive test conditions and stopping oracles from the machine's operating envelope
- Derive faults from design assumptions, physical hazards, and authority-transfer failures
- Select qualification environments that exercise the causal mechanism behind each claim
- Design hardware injections with independent witnesses and precommitted acceptance conditions
- Interpret temporal safety margins and search for disturbances that violate them
- Evaluate the assumptions limiting simulation transfer, rare-event estimates, and formal proofs
- Assemble fault records that preserve failed, invalid, unobservable, and untested cases

:::

## The Claim a Fault Trial Must Test {#sec-verification-fault-injection}

Every preceding chapter of this book culminates in concrete assertions about the running machine: a chunk lease that expires within its declared deadline, a deterministic permission path that halts the mobile base within its clear distance, a safety microcontroller that outlasts a voltage brownout on the shared electrical supply, or an authority arbiter that keeps a single writer on every channel while a handover is pending. The authority record that closed @sec-intervention can show weeks of clean handovers and still say nothing about a duplicate writer, a replayed packet, or a dropped heartbeat, because none occurred. Verification is the empirical discipline that converts these design assertions into auditable evidence. In embodied physical AI, the core verification challenge is distinct from purely digital software testing. The claims that matter most govern protective fallback responses that remain dormant until a subsystem breaks. Normal operation almost never exercises these safety paths, and an unexpected failure discovered in production has already crossed the causal boundary into the physical environment, releasing kinetic energy or risking collision that no subsequent software fix can undo. Protective safety mechanisms must therefore be provoked deliberately before release, under the severe physical conditions that make them necessary.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_as.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Act-to-Sense feedback edge."}

*A trial passes only when an independent sensor witnesses the act.*
:::

Policy evaluation measures how proficiently a learned candidate policy solves tasks across declared environments and operational conditions. Verification, by contrast, tests the integrated machine as a whole: proposer, runtime enforcer, communication buses, power distribution network, and physical body. High task completion rates during policy evaluation do not prove that an independent emergency stop executes reliably when the neural proposer hangs; conversely, an effective emergency stop does not demonstrate that the learned policy navigates aisles smoothly. Certifying an embodied system requires both forms of evidence collected on the exact same production hardware and software stack. This same distinction separates unconstrained policy autonomy from whole-machine operational success: an enforcer applying a least-change correction can keep the machine safe and productive during a mission while isolating and logging a dangerous proposal from the model.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** Policy evaluation, which scores the learned proposer's task proficiency rather than the whole machine's protective responses, is established in @sec-evaluation.
:::

The **digital twin delusion**\index{Digital twin delusion!simulation limits}[^fn-digital-twin-origin] treats passing assertions in a virtual simulator as sufficient proof of physical safety. A physics engine or digital emulator models timing jitter, power transients, and surface traction only to the extent that its authors anticipate and calibrate those effects. A simulated controller cannot fail on an unmodeled supply sag or bus collision. Passive operational logs encourage an equally dangerous complacency: millions of incident-free operating hours simply show that catastrophic corner conditions have not yet occurred during benign runs, leaving dormant failure modes unprobed.

[^fn-digital-twin-origin]: **Digital Twin**\index{Digital twin!origin}: @grieves2017digital trace the concept to a 2002 presentation on product lifecycle management, and @glaessgen2012digital gave it the sense aerospace adopted, a simulation of one as-built vehicle, updated continually from that vehicle's own sensors and history so that it mirrors the life of its flying twin. The original meaning therefore depended on continual calibration against one particular physical article. A simulator that has never been compared with a measured stop of this machine is a model, not a twin, and treating it as a twin is the delusion this chapter names.

Adversarial fault injection\index{Adversarial fault injection!definition} resolves this problem by turning an architectural claim into a controlled, deliberate disturbance executed under independent physical containment. To count as valid engineering evidence, a fault trial cannot be an ad hoc stress test; it must declare its operating-envelope point, evaluate telemetry against precommitted oracles that leave no room for subjective interpretation, and preserve cryptographic records of the hardware and software state. The campaign must then report which points across the envelope these trials cover. Hardware test cells must physically contain the machine's kinetic energy during injection while test harnesses capture the exact temporal propagation of the fault across power rails, fieldbuses, and mechanical brakes.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-rack-end-oracle
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RACK-END FAULT-INJECTION ORACLE FOR THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: fault-injection scene, operating envelope, fault list, oracles,
# │          hardware injection, fault manifest, fallacies, and summary.
# │ Goal: Derive the two oracle bounds (powered deceleration onset after the last valid renewal,
# │       stopping distance at the aisle speed) and the envelope points that
# │       F1-F4 and A1-A4 are injected at, all from the machine's registry entry.
# │ Show: 82 ms onset bound; 969.0 mm budget and 131.0 mm spare at 1.3 m/s;
# │       100.8 ms of travel in that spare, 751.6 ms at the 0.75 m/s takeover
# │       speed; the 1.44 m/s dry and 1.23 m/s inspected-floor ceilings; the
# │       37.8 V sustained drive-bus sag, 4.8 V above the 33 V converter
# │       lockout (150 A to cross it); the permission rail's 2.0 s hold-up against
# │       1313.43 ms from flag to brakes set (F4b); F1's stop oracle from the
# │       last valid renewal (751.9 mm at 1.3 m/s); the F1 record's oracle at
# │       the restricted 1.0 m/s point (629.6 mm from the last valid renewal);
# │       the Class 3 tank contrast (volume, not distance); F2's refusal
# │       threshold, the 51.6 ms budgeted dispatch age plus the 0.2 ms clock-conversion
# │       bound (51.8 ms upper age); the unbudgeted queue length that exhausts
# │       the spare (100.8 ms, about three-quarters of the pre-brake subtotal);
# │       a late-onset F1 trace's signed and normalized margins; the SoC's share
# │       of the bus transient (1.6 A of 70 A); the discrepancy a spare-sized
# │       simulated margin tolerates (0.131 in a 1 m position norm); the visible
# │       arithmetic of the reference-event notebook (217.1 mm between the capture-
# │       referenced subtotal and the F1 oracle) and the supply-headroom notebook
# │       (headroom vanishes near 129 mOhm); checkpoint givens (a 90 ms onset).
# │ How: the jerk-limited S-curve stop (calc_scurve_stop_distance / _time,
# │      calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity) with the jerk bound taken as the
# │      reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit, as in
# │      @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix, and the three fixed overheads;
# │      calc_voltage_droop for the 48 V drive bus (M6); tank arithmetic by
# │      conservation of volume.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, kilogram, microsecond, millisecond, second, meter, millimeter
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_stop_time,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
)
from mlsysim.physics import calc_voltage_droop
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_voltage,
    fmt_current,
    fmt_temperature,
    fmt_mass,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_power,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_resistance,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

def _num(q, unit, p):
    # Plain magnitude for the notebooks' visible arithmetic (no thousands separator inside math);
    # integer-like values print without a decimal, others at precision p
    x = q.to(unit).magnitude
    if abs(x - round(x)) < 1e-9:
        return fmt_int(round(x), commas=False)
    return fmt(x, precision=p, commas=False)

class RackEndVerification:
    """Oracle bounds and envelope points for fault injection at the rack end."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (clock-conversion bound, @sec-perception-observation-contract)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    heartbeat_timeout = AISLE.heartbeat_timeout  # category: chosen
    enforcer_deadline = AISLE.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_takeover = AISLE.t_takeover_in_loop  # category: derived (sourced reaction, video, and handshake terms; M4)
    v_takeover = AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop  # category: derived (Delta_da-charged in-loop ceiling, rounded down; Ch14)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    mu_dry = AISLE.mu_dry  # category: illustrative
    mu_insp = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative
    payload = RM.onboard_payload_capacity  # category: chosen
    bus_nominal = RM.drive_bus_nominal  # category: datasheet (48 V-class pack, nominal)
    bus_low = RM.drive_bus_battery_low  # category: datasheet (pack minimum)
    bus_r = RM.drive_bus_resistance  # category: illustrative (source path; needs a measured value)
    bus_uvlo = RM.drive_bus_uvlo  # category: datasheet (converter input lockout)
    i_rail = AISLE.i_rail_transient  # category: illustrative
    rail_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen
    brake_engage_max = RM.spring_brake_engage_max  # category: illustrative
    g = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # physical constant (defined); category: derived
    # Scenario assumptions local to this chapter
    ambient_lo = ureg.Quantity(5.0, ureg.degC)  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    ambient_hi = ureg.Quantity(35.0, ureg.degC)  # scenario assumption; category: chosen
    lease_probe = 5 * millisecond  # proposal injected after expiry; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    v_restricted = (
        1.0 * meter / second
    )  # candidate speed in the optimistic all-weight inspected-floor screen, below its ceiling; scenario assumption; category: chosen
    late_onset = 30 * millisecond  # example late powered deceleration onset (STL margin); scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    chk_onset = 90 * millisecond  # checkpoint given: a measured onset after the last valid renewal; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    soc_power = RM.brain_soc.tdp_max  # category: datasheet (application SoC maximum module power)
    converter_eff = RM.drive_bus_converter_efficiency  # category: datasheet (typical converter efficiency)
    drive_current_limit = RM.drive_current_limit  # category: chosen (per-motor datasheet peak)
    drive_wheels = RM.drive_wheel_count  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    # Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    onset_bound = (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    upper_age = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # F2: dispatch-only upper-age threshold; admission/execution age continues
    lease_probe_at = (t_lease + lease_probe).to(millisecond)
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    c2_distance = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    budget = (v_aisle * tau_delay + c2_distance + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    t_spare = (spare / v_aisle).to(millisecond)
    per_ms = (v_aisle * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    budget_takeover = (v_takeover * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_takeover, a_brake, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare_takeover = (d_clear - budget_takeover).to(millimeter)
    t_spare_takeover = (spare_takeover / v_takeover).to(millisecond)
    ceiling_dry = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    mu_min = float((a_brake / g).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Optimistic all-weight traction screen (phi_drive = 1), not loaded qualification.
    # The floor caps the deceleration; the jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
    a_insp = min(a_brake, (mu_insp * g).to(meter / second**2))
    budget_insp = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_insp, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    ceiling_insp = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_insp, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    bus_sag = calc_voltage_droop(i_rail, bus_r).to(ureg.volt)
    bus_min = (bus_low - bus_sag).to(ureg.volt)  # sustained screen from the depleted pack
    bus_margin = (bus_min - bus_uvlo).to(ureg.volt)
    i_cross = ((bus_low - bus_uvlo) / bus_r).to(ureg.ampere)  # step that would reach the lockout
    # F4: from the undervoltage or feed-loss flag, stop onset, the longest resident
    # stop in this screening branch (inspected floor at its optimistic ceiling), and brakes set
    flag_onset = (t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    stop_insp_ceiling = calc_scurve_stop_time(ceiling_insp, a_insp, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    flag_to_set = (flag_onset + stop_insp_ceiling + brake_engage_max).to(millisecond)
    holdup_margin = (rail_holdup - flag_to_set).to(millisecond)
    # F1 record at the restricted point, scored from the last valid renewal
    f1_preonset = (v_restricted * onset_bound).to(millimeter)
    f1_c2 = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_restricted, a_insp, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    f1_stop_bound = (f1_preonset + f1_c2 + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    # F1 at the aisle speed, scored from the same event (last valid renewal)
    f1_aisle_stop_bound = (v_aisle * onset_bound + c2_distance + eps_track).to(millimeter)
    budget_restricted = (v_restricted * tau_delay + f1_c2 + overhead).to(millimeter)
    late_extra = (v_aisle * late_onset).to(millimeter)
    # Signed margins of one late-onset F1 trace against the renewal-referenced oracle
    onset_late = (onset_bound + late_onset).to(millisecond)
    travel_nominal = (v_aisle * onset_bound + c2_distance).to(millimeter)
    travel_late = (travel_nominal + late_extra).to(millimeter)
    rho_onset = (onset_bound - onset_late).to(millisecond)
    rho_dist = (f1_aisle_stop_bound - travel_late).to(millimeter)
    # Normalized by chosen scales equal to the bounds themselves
    rho_onset_n = float((rho_onset / onset_bound).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    rho_dist_n = float((rho_dist / f1_aisle_stop_bound).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Notebook nbk-verification-reference-event-gap: both sums term by term
    f1_preonset_aisle = (v_aisle * onset_bound).to(millimeter)
    capture_preonset = (v_aisle * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    age_travel = (v_aisle * t_age).to(millimeter)
    ref_gap = (budget - f1_aisle_stop_bound).to(millimeter)
    late_equiv = (ref_gap / v_aisle).to(millisecond)  # onset slip the distance predicate alone would absorb
    sfx_v2 = (v_aisle**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(meter)  # d_suffix, braking term (@eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix)
    sfx_jerk = (v_aisle * a_brake / (2 * j_brake)).to(meter)  # d_suffix, jerk-ramp term
    sfx_v2_r = (v_restricted**2 / (2 * a_insp)).to(meter)
    sfx_jerk_r = (v_restricted * a_insp / (2 * j_brake)).to(meter)
    speed_cut = 1.0 - float((v_restricted / v_aisle).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    oracle_cut = 1.0 - float((f1_stop_bound / f1_aisle_stop_bound).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Notebook nbk-verification-supply-headroom: stop time T = v/a + a/j from the inspected-floor ceiling
    tstop_va = (ceiling_insp / a_insp).to(millisecond)
    tstop_aj = (a_insp / j_brake).to(millisecond)
    r_cross = ((bus_low - bus_uvlo) / i_rail).to(ureg.milliohm)  # source resistance at which the transient alone reaches lockout
    step_ratio = float((i_cross / i_rail).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Checkpoint given: onset and pre-braking travel of a late F1 onset
    chk_rho = (onset_bound - chk_onset).to(millisecond)
    chk_extra = (v_aisle * (chk_onset - onset_bound)).to(millimeter)
    # Shared-bus sag attribution: the application SoC's maximum draw from the depleted bus
    soc_current = (soc_power / (bus_low * converter_eff)).to(ureg.ampere)
    drive_peak = (drive_current_limit * drive_wheels).to(ureg.ampere)
    soc_share = float((soc_current / i_rail).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Sim-to-real instance: position error in meters (L_phi = 1 m per unit of the norm);
    # a simulated margin equal to the spare tolerates at most this discrepancy
    eps_gap_max = float((spare / (1 * meter)).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    # Fallacy: an unbudgeted queue spends the spare at v per unit time, so the
    # queue length that exhausts it is the spare's travel time t_spare.
    queue_exhaust_ratio = (t_spare / tau_delay).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(onset_bound.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: powered deceleration onset 82 ms after the last valid renewal.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 5e-3, "Canon: tau_delay 133.6 ms.")
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 5e-3, "Canon: t_age 51.6 ms.")
    check(abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, "Clock-conversion bound must match the perception contract's 0.2 ms.")
    check(abs(upper_age.magnitude - 51.8) < 5e-3, "Canon (D22): F2 dispatch-age check refuses above a 51.8 ms upper age.")
    check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: the jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak.")
    check(abs(budget.magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, "Canon: budget at 1.3 m/s is 968.99 mm.")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, "Canon: spare at 1.3 m/s is 131.01 mm.")
    check(abs(c2_distance.magnitude - 605.3125) < 5e-3, "Canon: S-curve stop at 1.3 m/s is 605.31 mm.")
    check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Canon: T_latest 100.8 ms.")
    check(abs(ceiling_dry.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Canon: dry-floor ceiling 1.4367 m/s.")
    check(abs(ceiling_insp.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Canon: inspected-floor ceiling 1.2309 m/s.")
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Canon: friction needed for a_brake is 0.204.")
    check(abs(bus_min.magnitude - 37.8) < 5e-3, "Canon: the depleted drive bus sags to 37.8 V.")
    check(abs(bus_margin.magnitude - 4.8) < 5e-3, "The sustained screen leaves 4.8 V above the converter lockout.")
    check(abs(i_cross.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-6, "Reaching the lockout takes a 150 A step.")
    check(bus_min > bus_uvlo, "The load alone cannot cross the lockout, so F4a must inject a supply dip.")
    check(v_aisle < ceiling_dry and ceiling_insp < v_aisle, "Aisle speed sits between the two ceilings.")
    check(budget_insp > d_clear, "At the aisle speed the inspected-floor budget must exceed the clear distance.")
    check(mu_insp < mu_min < mu_dry, "The all-weight screen permits a_brake on dry floor, not inspected floor.")
    check(t_spare < tau_delay, "A queue shorter than the budgeted pre-brake subtotal exhausts the spare.")
    check(abs(queue_exhaust_ratio - 0.754) < 5e-4, "The exhausting queue is about three-quarters of the pre-brake subtotal.")
    check(abs(overhead.magnitude - 190.0) < 1e-6, "Canon: fixed overhead 190 mm.")
    check(
        rho_onset.magnitude < 0 and abs(rho_dist.magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "The nominal late trace fails onset but retains 1 mm of distance allowance."
    )
    check(abs(rho_onset_n + 30.0 / 82.0) < 1e-9, "Normalized onset margin is -30/82.")
    check(rho_onset_n < 0 < rho_dist_n, "Only the onset predicate fails in the nominal trace.")
    check(soc_current < 0.05 * i_rail, "The SoC draws a few percent of the rail transient; drive current dominates.")
    check(drive_peak <= i_rail, "Two drive motors at their peak supply most of the transient.")
    check(abs(eps_gap_max - spare.to(meter).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Tolerable discrepancy equals the spare in meters.")
    check(abs(v_takeover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.75) < 1e-9, "Canon: in-loop takeover speed 0.75 m/s (derived, Ch14).")
    check(
        t_spare_takeover >= t_takeover + AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission, "At the slowed speed the spare must cover the in-loop takeover and Delta_da."
    )
    check(t_spare < t_takeover, "At the aisle speed the spare cannot cover the in-loop takeover.")
    check(abs(spare_takeover.magnitude - 563.71) < 5e-2, "Canon: spare at the 0.75 m/s takeover speed is 563.7 mm.")
    check(abs(t_spare_takeover.magnitude - 751.6) < 5e-2, "Canon: T_latest 751.6 ms at 0.75 m/s.")
    check(abs(flag_onset.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: stop onset within 22 ms of the flag.")
    check(abs(rail_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Canon: permission-rail hold-up 2.0 s.")
    check(abs(flag_to_set.magnitude - 1313.43) < 5e-3, "Canon: flag to brakes set 1313.43 ms.")
    check(abs(holdup_margin.magnitude - 686.57) < 5e-3, "Canon: hold-up margin 686.57 ms.")
    check(v_restricted < ceiling_insp, "The restricted point must sit below the inspected-floor ceiling.")
    check(abs(f1_preonset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-6, "Canon: 82 mm of pre-onset travel at 1.0 m/s.")
    check(abs(f1_c2.magnitude - 507.6) < 5e-2, "Canon: S-curve stop at 1.0 m/s on the inspected floor is 507.6 mm.")
    check(abs(f1_stop_bound.magnitude - 629.6) < 5e-2, "Canon: F1 stop oracle 629.6 mm from the last valid renewal.")
    check(
        abs(f1_aisle_stop_bound.magnitude - 751.9125) < 5e-3 and f1_aisle_stop_bound < budget,
        "F1 stop oracle at 1.3 m/s is 751.91 mm from the last valid renewal.",
    )
    check(
        abs(budget_restricted.magnitude - 831.2) < 5e-2 and budget_restricted < d_clear,
        "Canon: budget at 1.0 m/s on the inspected floor is 831.2 mm.",
    )
    # margin_renewal_onset_deadline_bar.svg fig-alt hand-types 60, 1, 1, and 20 ms (82 ms guarded above)
    check(
        abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9
        and abs(t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9
        and abs(t_bus.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9
        and abs(t_act.to(millisecond).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9,
        "Onset-bar fig-alt: lease 60 ms, tick 1 ms, bus 1 ms, onset 20 ms.",
    )
    # margin_floor_friction_ceiling_knee.svg fig-alt hand-types mu 0.12 and 1.3 m/s (0.204, 1.44, 1.23 guarded above)
    check(abs(mu_insp - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Knee fig-alt: mu 0.12, aisle 1.3 m/s.")
    # Reference-event notebook: the closed-form stop matches the MLSysIM S-curve, and the
    # capture-referenced subtotal exceeds the F1 oracle by exactly age travel plus the two margins
    check(abs((sfx_v2 + sfx_jerk).to(millimeter).magnitude - c2_distance.magnitude) < 1e-6, "d_suffix = v^2/2a + v a/2j at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(abs((sfx_v2_r + sfx_jerk_r).to(millimeter).magnitude - f1_c2.magnitude) < 1e-6, "d_suffix = v^2/2a + v a/2j at 1.0 m/s.")
    check(v_restricted > a_insp**2 / j_brake and v_aisle > a_brake**2 / j_brake, "Both stops reach the deceleration plateau.")
    check(
        abs(ref_gap.magnitude - (age_travel + delta_loc + delta_margin).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "Gap = age travel + delta_loc + delta_margin.",
    )
    check(
        abs(ref_gap.magnitude - 217.08) < 5e-3 and 2 * onset_bound < late_equiv < 2.1 * onset_bound,
        "The 217.1 mm gap hides about twice the onset bound.",
    )
    check(abs(speed_cut - 0.231) < 5e-4 and abs(oracle_cut - 0.163) < 5e-4, "A 23 percent slower point shortens the oracle 16 percent.")
    check(abs((tstop_va + tstop_aj - stop_insp_ceiling).magnitude) < 1e-6, "Stop time T = v/a + a/j at the inspected ceiling.")
    check(
        abs(r_cross.magnitude - 128.571) < 5e-3 and 2.0 < step_ratio < 2.2,
        "Headroom vanishes near 129 mOhm; the crossing step is about twice the transient.",
    )
    check(
        rho_onset_n < float((rho_dist / eps_track).to("dimensionless").magnitude),
        "Checkpoint: onset still sets the combined score with the tracking inset as distance scale.",
    )
    check(abs(chk_rho.magnitude + 8.0) < 1e-9 and abs(chk_extra.magnitude - 10.4) < 1e-6, "Checkpoint: 90 ms onset misses by 8 ms and adds 10.4 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=None)
    a_insp_str = fmt_acceleration(a_insp, precision=2)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

    upper_age_str = fmt_latency(upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=None)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=None)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    onset_bound_str = fmt_latency(onset_bound, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    lease_probe_at_str = fmt_latency(lease_probe_at, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    heartbeat_timeout_str = fmt_latency(heartbeat_timeout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    enforcer_deadline_str = fmt_latency(enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_takeover_str = fmt_latency(t_takeover, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    t_spare_takeover_str = fmt_latency(t_spare_takeover, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    per_ms_str = fmt_length(per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)

    ceiling_insp_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_insp, precision=2)

    mu_insp_str = fmt(mu_insp, precision=2)
    payload_str = fmt_mass(payload, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    ambient_lo_str = fmt_temperature(ambient_lo, precision=0)
    ambient_hi_str = fmt_temperature(ambient_hi, precision=0)

    bus_low_str = fmt_voltage(bus_low, precision=0)
    bus_uvlo_str = fmt_voltage(bus_uvlo, precision=0)

    # Notebook, checkpoint, and definition strings
    j_brake_str = fmt(j_brake.magnitude, precision=2)
    eps_track_str = fmt_length(eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    ref_gap_str = fmt_length(ref_gap, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    age_travel_str = fmt_length(age_travel, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    late_equiv_str = fmt_latency(round(late_equiv.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)  # displayed as "about"
    speed_cut_pct_str = fmt_percent(speed_cut, precision=1, style="prose")
    oracle_cut_pct_str = fmt_percent(oracle_cut, precision=1, style="prose")
    chk_onset_str = fmt_latency(chk_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    bus_r_str = fmt_resistance(bus_r, unit=ureg.milliohm, precision=0)
    brake_engage_str = fmt_latency(brake_engage_max, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    holdup_margin_str = fmt_latency(holdup_margin, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    r_cross_str = fmt_resistance(round(r_cross.magnitude) * ureg.milliohm, unit=ureg.milliohm, precision=0)  # displayed as "about"
    _ms, _mm, _mps, _mps2 = millisecond, millimeter, meter / second, meter / second**2
    onset_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{onset}}}} \le T_{{\text{{lease}}}} + T_{{\text{{tick}}}} + T_{{\text{{bus}}}} + T_{{\text{{act}}}}"
        rf" = {_num(t_lease, _ms, 0)} + {_num(t_tick, _ms, 0)} + {_num(t_bus, _ms, 0)} + {_num(t_act, _ms, 0)}"
        rf" = {_num(onset_bound, _ms, 0)}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    suffix_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{suffix}}}}(v) = \frac{{v^2}}{{2a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}} + \frac{{v\,a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}}{{2j_{{\max}}}}"
        rf" = \frac{{{_num(v_aisle, _mps, 1)}^2}}{{2 \times {_num(a_brake, _mps2, 1)}}}"
        rf" + \frac{{{_num(v_aisle, _mps, 1)} \times {_num(a_brake, _mps2, 1)}}}{{2 \times {j_brake_str}}}"
        rf" = {_num(sfx_v2, meter, 4)} + {_num(sfx_jerk, meter, 4)} = {_num(sfx_v2 + sfx_jerk, meter, 4)}\ \text{{m}}"
    )
    f1_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{F1}}}}(v) = {_num(v_aisle, _mps, 1)} \times {_num(onset_bound, _ms, 0)} + {_num(c2_distance, _mm, 1)} + {_num(eps_track, _mm, 0)}"
        rf" = {_num(f1_preonset_aisle, _mm, 1)} + {_num(c2_distance, _mm, 1)} + {_num(eps_track, _mm, 0)}"
        rf" = {_num(f1_aisle_stop_bound, _mm, 1)}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    capture_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"v\,\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} + d_{{\text{{suffix}}}} + \delta_{{\text{{loc}}}} + \delta_{{\text{{margin}}}} + \epsilon_{{\text{{track}}}}"
        rf" = {_num(v_aisle, _mps, 1)} \times {_num(tau_delay, _ms, 1)} + {_num(c2_distance, _mm, 1)} + {_num(delta_loc, _mm, 0)} + {_num(delta_margin, _mm, 0)} + {_num(eps_track, _mm, 0)}"
        rf" = {_num(budget, _mm, 1)}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    gap_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"{_num(budget, _mm, 1)} - {_num(f1_aisle_stop_bound, _mm, 1)} = {_num(v_aisle, _mps, 1)} \times {_num(t_age, _ms, 1)} + {_num(delta_loc, _mm, 0)} + {_num(delta_margin, _mm, 0)}"
        rf" = {_num(age_travel, _mm, 1)} + {_num(delta_loc + delta_margin, _mm, 0)} = {_num(ref_gap, _mm, 1)}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    restricted_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{F1}}}}({_num(v_restricted, _mps, 1)}) = {_num(v_restricted, _mps, 1)} \times {_num(onset_bound, _ms, 0)}"
        rf" + \left(\frac{{{_num(v_restricted, _mps, 1)}^2}}{{2 \times {_num(a_insp, _mps2, 3)}}} + \frac{{{_num(v_restricted, _mps, 1)} \times {_num(a_insp, _mps2, 3)}}}{{2 \times {j_brake_str}}}\right)\text{{m}}"
        rf" + {_num(eps_track, _mm, 0)} = {_num(f1_preonset, _mm, 1)} + {_num(f1_c2, _mm, 1)} + {_num(eps_track, _mm, 0)} = {_num(f1_stop_bound, _mm, 1)}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    sag_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"V_{{\min}} = V_{{\text{{low}}}} - I\,R = {_num(bus_low, ureg.volt, 1)} - {_num(i_rail, ureg.ampere, 0)} \times {_num(bus_r, ureg.ohm, 3)}"
        rf" = {_num(bus_min, ureg.volt, 1)}\ \text{{V}}, \qquad I_{{\text{{cross}}}} = \frac{{V_{{\text{{low}}}} - V_{{\text{{UVLO}}}}}}{{R}}"
        rf" = \frac{{{_num(bus_low, ureg.volt, 1)} - {_num(bus_uvlo, ureg.volt, 0)}}}{{{_num(bus_r, ureg.ohm, 3)}}} = {_num(i_cross, ureg.ampere, 0)}\ \text{{A}}"
    )
    holdup_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{set}}}} = (T_{{\text{{tick}}}} + T_{{\text{{bus}}}} + T_{{\text{{act}}}}) + \left(\frac{{v}}{{a}} + \frac{{a}}{{j_{{\max}}}}\right) + t_{{\text{{engage}}}}"
        rf" = {_num(flag_onset, _ms, 0)} + \left(\frac{{{_num(ceiling_insp, _mps, 3)}}}{{{_num(a_insp, _mps2, 3)}}} + \frac{{{_num(a_insp, _mps2, 3)}}}{{{j_brake_str}}}\right)\text{{s}} + {_num(brake_engage_max, _ms, 0)}"
        rf" = {_num(flag_onset, _ms, 0)} + {_num(tstop_va, _ms, 1)} + {_num(tstop_aj, _ms, 1)} + {_num(brake_engage_max, _ms, 0)} = {_num(flag_to_set, _ms, 1)}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-admission-charge
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE DISPATCH-TO-ADMISSION CHARGE AGAINST THE RACK-END SPARE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-verification-operating-envelope (stopping-budget paragraph),
# │          @fig-15-reference-events, the A3 paragraph of
# │          @sec-verification-forward-analysis, @tbl-15-fault-classification
# │          (F4a row), @sec-verification-hardware-timing-search, and
# │          @sec-verification-importance-sampling.
# │ Goal: Charge the allocated dispatch-to-admission interval of
# │       @sec-placement-dispatch-admission to the aisle-speed spare, as the
# │       placement and intervention chapters do, and give F4a a distance bound
# │       from its flag for the case in which the drives keep their authority.
# │ Show: 63.3 ms allocation; 82.3 mm of travel at 1.3 m/s; 48.7 mm and
# │       37.5 ms of the 131.0 mm / 100.8 ms spare left; F4a bound from the
# │       flag 673.9 mm (22 ms onset, resident stop, tracking inset).
# │ How: Delta_da is AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission (MLSysIM), an allocation,
# │      not a measurement; remainders by subtraction from RackEndVerification.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, millimeter
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, check

class AdmissionChargeVerification:
    """The allocated dispatch-to-admission interval charged to the aisle-speed spare."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    R = RackEndVerification  # category: derived; calc in this chapter's oracle cell
    delta_da = (
        Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle.t_dispatch_to_admission
    )  # category: illustrative (allocation of @sec-placement-dispatch-admission, not a measurement)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    travel_da = (R.v_aisle * delta_da).to(millimeter)
    spare_left = (R.spare - travel_da).to(millimeter)
    t_left = (R.t_spare - delta_da).to(millisecond)
    # F4a with surviving drive authority: flag-referenced onset, resident stop, tracking inset
    f4a_bound = (R.v_aisle * R.flag_onset + R.c2_distance + R.eps_track).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(delta_da.to(millisecond).magnitude - 63.3) < 0.05, "Canon: Delta_da allocation 63.3 ms.")
    check(abs(travel_da.magnitude - 82.3) < 0.05, "Delta_da costs 82.3 mm at the aisle speed.")
    check(abs(spare_left.magnitude - 48.7) < 0.05, "Canon: 48.7 mm of the spare survive the charge.")
    check(abs(t_left.magnitude - 37.5) < 0.05, "Canon: 37.5 ms of waiting survive the charge at the aisle speed.")
    check(delta_da < R.t_spare, "The allocation must fit inside the spare-exhausting ceiling.")
    check(abs(f4a_bound.magnitude - 673.9) < 0.05 and f4a_bound < R.f1_aisle_stop_bound, "F4a bound from the flag is 673.9 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_da_str = fmt_length(travel_da, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_left_str = fmt_length(spare_left, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_left_str = fmt_latency(t_left, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f4a_bound_str = fmt_length(f4a_bound, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

Consider the warehouse mobile manipulator navigating an aisle at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) toward a rack end where a pedestrian may step out from a blind intersection. The learned proposer might abruptly stop renewing motion commands while the base continues rolling under momentum. An architectural authority diagram specifies which subsystem must take over, but that specification does not prove that the physical permission path survives the crash or that mechanical brakes engage before impact. An empirical trial that induces the fault and measures physical motion supplies evidence for the named protective response under its declared conditions. To structure that trial, the test harness must reflect how the machine partitions execution across its physical substrates: an application system-on-chip (SoC) equipped with an embedded accelerator executes the unprivileged learned proposers (the vision-language-action intent model and the chunk policy beneath it), while a lockstep safety microcontroller executes the deterministic runtime enforcer. The safety microcontroller commands the base-drive motor inverters across a hard real-time fieldbus (EtherCAT, or Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate, CAN FD) whose cyclic frames arrive on a strict, microsecond-scale schedule. Both processors draw power from the shared `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str` drive bus that powers the traction motors: the application SoC through a buck-boost converter, and the safety microcontroller through an isolated converter backed by a dedicated, held-up permission rail.

Weeks of uneventful operational logs at that speed say little about four severe hardware and timing faults that the architecture claims to contain:

1. **Proposer Stall (F1):** The chunk policy, the fast proposer of @sec-brain-two-proposers that renews motion every `{python} RackEndVerification.chunk_period_str`, has its latest proposal successfully admitted by the permission path, renewing its chunk lease, but immediately suffers a thread deadlock, driver lockup, or thermal throttling freeze.
2. **Stale Observation (F2):** A camera frame or depth tensor arrives at the permission path with an aged or corrupted hardware timestamp after silent queuing in an image signal processor (ISP) buffer or direct memory access (DMA) ring.
3. **Lost Fieldbus Frames (F3):** Electromagnetic interference (EMI) from high-current inverter switching corrupts or drops a burst of EtherCAT or CAN FD frames between the safety microcontroller and the wheel actuators.
4. **Drive-Bus Droop and Feed Loss (F4a/F4b):** A supply injector steps the shared `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str` drive bus below the `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_uvlo_str` lockout threshold of the converter feeding the application processor under the declared drive load (F4a), or the permission rail itself loses its primary electrical feed (F4b).

These physical failure modes F1–F4, paired with the supervisory authority transfer faults A1–A4 (formalized in @tbl-15-fault-classification), organize the entire verification campaign. In theory, each threat has a dedicated countermeasure: the lease detects a hung proposer, the evidence-epoch check discards stale sensor frames, the fieldbus watchdog flags dropped communication cycles, and the isolated undervoltage supervisor manages electrical brownouts. In practice, adversarial verification injects each disturbance as the robot approaches the rack end, alongside the four authority handoff faults that the authority record hands over (@sec-intervention-evidence-tuples), and scores every stopping trial against temporal and distance bounds derived from the machine's own stopping budget.

An injected fault converts a physical trial into valid evidence for an auditable safety case only when the experiment satisfies the five requirements of the **cyber-physical test contract**:

1. **A bounded claim:** The test specifies the exact invariant the machine must maintain. For the mobile base at the rack end, the machine must come to a complete stop within the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clear distance.
2. **Defined test conditions:** The specification bounds every relevant physical variable, including initial velocity, payload mass, floor friction, ambient operating temperature, bus traffic saturation, and DC supply voltages.
3. **A precommitted oracle\index{Testing!Oracle}:** An automated evaluation harness inspects captured telemetry against the claim without human intervention, retrospective threshold tuning, or post-hoc excuses (@sec-verification-oracles-acceptance defines the oracle formally).
4. **A stated sampling and injection procedure:** The test harness exercises the machine systematically across its operational envelope, deliberately triggering faults in sensors, buses, power rails, and actuators during peak mechanical and computational load.
5. **Provenance\index{Provenance}:** The campaign logs complete cryptographic digests of model weights, calibration tables, sensor serial numbers, oscilloscope traces, and raw bus logs to enable matched re-execution. Software builds can be reproduced bit for bit; a physical trial can be replicated only when repeated under physical conditions that match declared tolerances.

The base's stopping claim and the manipulator arm's latch-force claim require separate operational envelopes, injection points, and acceptance criteria; this chapter follows the mobile base's stopping claim. Fixing the contract starts with its second element, the declared conditions under which the claim must hold, which also locate the point beyond which nominal regulation must yield to an independent containment response.

## The Operating Envelope {#sec-verification-operating-envelope}

An operating envelope couples the external operational design domain (ODD) with the internal execution state of the computing and actuation hardware. A mobile robot carrying a full payload down a warehouse aisle behaves very differently when memory bus contention delays perception pipelines, when battery supply rails sag under acceleration, or when drive inverters heat up under sustained torque. Empirical verification is therefore meaningless without specifying both dimensions: every protective claim must declare the environmental bounds and the internal computational and electrical loads under which it is guaranteed to hold.

For the mobile manipulator, the operating envelope declares the range of conditions over which the protective claim must hold. The campaign samples a discrete set of qualification points within that range; extending their results to untested points requires an explicit coverage argument. These points span an aisle speed of `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str`, payload masses ranging from an unloaded chassis to the full `{python} RackEndVerification.payload_str` rack capacity, and ambient operating temperatures from `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_lo_str` to `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_hi_str`. Surface friction must also be parameterized explicitly. In an optimistic all-weight traction screen, dry aisles require a friction coefficient of at least `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_min_str` to support the design braking deceleration of `{python} RackEndVerification.a_brake_str`, whereas areas under the facility floor inspection regime guarantee only `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str`. The screen assumes that the driven wheels carry the entire weight; the actual base requires a qualified loaded deceleration that respects driven-wheel load share, configured braking current, and tip stability. For these inspected surfaces, the screen identifies a candidate restricted point at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str`, whose friction premise must be logged in the enforcement telemetry. Verification trials on inspected floors must run against a physical test surface calibrated to this `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` threshold and must recalculate the oracles from the qualified loaded deceleration before testing the actual base.

Each physical configuration couples directly to the machine's internal execution state. Trials must evaluate application-processor utilization driven to peak neural inference bursts, drive-bus voltages sweeping from a depleted `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_low_str` up to a nominal `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str`, transmission jitter across EtherCAT or CAN FD buses, DRAM crossbar contention, and the thermal state of the safety microcontroller. The verification campaign also challenges transient edge conditions, chief among them a human takeover while the base is moving. @Sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines screens a candidate in-loop takeover, with its `{python} RackEndVerification.t_takeover_str` conservative response-and-exchange allowance, at the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_takeover_str` slow-down; the same moving handover is infeasible at the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed and must be rejected. The slow-down remains a qualification candidate, conditional on operator response, admission delay, current clearance, and a feasible stopping continuation. The operative design stops the base before handing over. Both speeds therefore belong in the campaign, one to challenge a candidate moving transition and one to verify its rejection. The system must enforce a local stop whenever an authority transition cannot safely preserve the verified stopping envelope.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The rule that an authority transition unable to preserve the stopping envelope ends in a local stop is established in @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines.
:::

::: {#dfn-verification-operating-envelope .callout-definition title="Operating envelope"}

***Operating envelope***\index{Operating envelope!definition} is the declared set of external conditions and internal execution states, each point stated with its units and tolerances, over which a machine's protective claim must hold and at which every trial of that claim is run.

1.  **Significance**: The envelope governs which terms of the inequality $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ are stressed during an empirical trial. For the running machine, an aisle speed of `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` falls below the optimistic `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_dry_str` ceiling on a dry floor, yet exceeds the `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str` ceiling on an inspected surface. The identical velocity therefore passes the all-weight screen on one surface and fails it on another; passing still requires loaded qualification before admission.
2.  **Distinction**: The operational design domain describes the external environment encountered by the planning policy. The operating envelope expands this definition to incorporate internal machine states, including processor utilization, drive-bus voltages between `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_low_str` and `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str`, and communication bus saturation. The same physical aisle yields vastly different safety margins under memory contention or electrical depletion.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent mistake is treating an operating envelope as a simple Cartesian product of decoupled intervals, assuming that testing each parameter independently at its minimum and maximum guarantees coverage. In cyber-physical systems, multi-dimensional boundary couplings are the rule rather than the exception: two parameters operating well within their nominal isolated bounds can combine to trigger an unrecoverable failure. Robust verification demands testing directly at these coupled, high-stress corners.

:::

An operating envelope must be distinguished from the wider **survival envelope**\index{Survival envelope!definition} that encloses it. Within the operating envelope, the learned policy and low-level tracking controllers regulate nominal behavior. When an external disturbance, sensor dropout, or compute stall pushes the machine across that boundary, nominal control yields to safety mechanisms that bring the robot to a bounded, safe stop before structural limits are violated. For the mobile manipulator, the survival envelope must be characterized separately for each fallback response and machine state. The standard resident stop executes controlled, powered deceleration before setting electromechanical holding brakes at zero velocity. In contrast, torque inhibit prevents commanded torque generation without necessarily electrically isolating the drive; it does not follow the controlled stopping profile or inherit its stopping-distance budget. If the remaining containment mechanisms cannot absorb the motion, structural damage may result when kinetic energy ($\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \Mass \ImpactSpeed^2$) exceeds what mechanical compliance and chassis end-stop dampening can absorb before hard impact. For the base in a test cell, the survival envelope is therefore the set of states from which the qualified combination of torque inhibit, passive resistance, holding mechanisms, and compliant end-stops can contain the remaining motion and energy. That boundary, not the clear distance of the stopping claim, is what the test cell's own protection watches.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The fallback rungs, from the controlled resident stop to hardware torque inhibit, are established in @sec-enforcement-four-rungs.
:::

Establishing envelope boundaries requires deriving physical constraints from first principles rather than asserting arbitrary software timeouts. In rack-end operations, this boundary is governed by the stopping budget. Total stopping distance scales linearly with pre-braking latency and quadratically with vehicle speed (@eq-body-stopping-distance). In the conditional design budget of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget, a pre-brake subtotal of `{python} RackEndVerification.tau_delay_str` measured from sensor capture, combined with the jerk-limited resident stop and the tracking inset, yields a partial-budget speed ceiling of `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_dry_str` on a dry floor. That ceiling holds only before the dispatch-to-admission interval is charged, and @sec-placement-dispatch-admission allocated that interval without yet measuring it. Running at the candidate aisle velocity of `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` consumes `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` of the available `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clearance. The unallocated spare of `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str`, which the vehicle crosses in `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, must still absorb that interval. Its allocation of `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.delta_da_str` costs `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.travel_da_str` of travel at this speed and leaves `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.spare_left_str`, or `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.t_left_str` of waiting, the same remainder that @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines found for a human takeover at aisle speed. The full `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str` is therefore a ceiling, the longest dispatch-to-admission interval the spare could pay for. When later examples in this chapter quote the full spare, they quote an upper bound on the unbudgeted delay the machine can tolerate; once the allocation is charged, only the remainder is left to spend.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The jerk-limited resident stop and its stopping distance are established in @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix.
:::

Two conditional oracle bounds follow from that budget. Before any qualification trial, the harness must show that the bounds cover the whole execution path from the reference event to rest, because an interval left unallocated is an open qualification gap rather than a margin.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_renewal_onset_deadline_bar.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Stacked bar spanning the 82 milliseconds from the last valid renewal to powered deceleration onset: a 60 milliseconds lease, a 1 millisecond tick and a 1 millisecond bus cycle, and 20 milliseconds from delivered stop command to drive onset."}

*Of the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` onset deadline, the lease takes `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str`.*
:::

1. **Powered Deceleration Onset Deadline:** Powered deceleration must begin no later than `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` after the last valid renewal. This deadline traverses the full permission and actuation chain: the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str` lease duration, a single `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` tick of the safety permission loop, one `{python} RackEndVerification.t_bus_str` communication bus cycle, and the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_act_str` drive latency from delivered stop command to physical deceleration onset. (For the power-rail fault scenario F4, the onset deadline is referenced instead to the assertion of the hardware undervoltage flag.)
2. **Stopping Distance Bound:** The vehicle, tracked by external optical instruments independent of onboard odometry, must come to rest within the distance allocated from the reference event that triggers the fault. Three reference events are possible, and @fig-15-reference-events places them on one time axis. A *capture-referenced* trial measures clearance and displacement from the exposure midpoint of a qualified sensor capture; the `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` subtotal starts there but omits the dispatch-to-admission interval, so it is incomplete until that interval is added. An *appearance-referenced* trial starts earlier, at the optical appearance of an unheralded hazard; it must timestamp that appearance and the first usable capture independently, and add the travel between them, as well as the dispatch-to-admission travel, to obtain a complete bound against the clearance measured at appearance. A *renewal-referenced* trial applies when a stalled proposer produces no new target at all; it scores both stopping distance and onset latency from the last valid lease renewal. No trial may claim a pass against an incomplete budget subtotal.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The lease path, from the last admission through the permission tick and bus cycle to brake onset, is established in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing.
:::

Measured from that event, the two F1 verification predicates are (@eq-verification-f1-oracle):
$$\HazardOnset \le \ChunkLease + \PermissionLoopPeriod + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime, \qquad \StallTravelBound(\SpeedAtDetection) = \SpeedAtDetection\,(\ChunkLease + \PermissionLoopPeriod + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime) + \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) + \TrackingErrorBound$$ {#eq-verification-f1-oracle}
Here $\HazardOnset$ is the measured interval from the last valid renewal to the physical onset of powered deceleration, $\StallTravelBound(\SpeedAtDetection)$ bounds the measured travel from that renewal to rest, $\ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)$ is the jerk-limited resident stop profile from @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix, and $\TrackingErrorBound$ is the tracking inset. The design budget's pre-brake subtotal $\PrebrakeDelay$ begins earlier, at raw sensor capture, and its sum also carries the localization bound and the protective margin. Notebook \ref{nbk-verification-reference-event-gap} evaluates both sums at the rack end.

::: {#nbk-verification-reference-event-gap .callout-notebook title="The reference-event gap"}

**Problem**: A proposer stall at the aisle speed is scored from the last valid renewal. What onset and travel bounds follow from the lease path and the resident stop, and how far below the capture-referenced subtotal of the design budget do they sit?

**Variables**:

* $\SpeedAtDetection =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` (Chosen) and $\ClearDistance =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` (Illustrative; @tbl-01-machine-card).
* $\ChunkLease =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str` and $\PermissionLoopPeriod =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` (Chosen); $\CommandTransportTime =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_bus_str` and $\ActuatorResponseTime =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_act_str` (Illustrative).
* $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.a_brake_str` (Illustrative; stands in for a measured loaded deceleration) and $\JerkLimit =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.j_brake_str` m/s³ (Derived; the reference stop polynomial's peak jerk).
* $\TrackingErrorBound =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_track_str` and $\LocalizationBound =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.delta_loc_str` (Illustrative); $\ProtectiveClearanceMargin =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.delta_margin_str` (Chosen); evidence age $\ObservationAge =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_age_str` (Derived; @sec-perception-latency-waterfall).

**Math**:

*Onset bound.*
`{python} RackEndVerification.onset_math`

*Resident stop* (@eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix).
`{python} RackEndVerification.suffix_math`

*F1 oracle from the last valid renewal* (@eq-verification-f1-oracle).
`{python} RackEndVerification.f1_math`

*Capture-referenced subtotal*, which leaves `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` of the clear distance.
`{python} RackEndVerification.capture_math`

*The gap between them.*
`{python} RackEndVerification.gap_math`

*Sensitivity.* In the optimistic all-weight screen at the restricted point on the inspected floor, friction caps the deceleration at `{python} RackEndVerification.a_insp_str`:
`{python} RackEndVerification.restricted_math`
A speed reduction of `{python} RackEndVerification.speed_cut_pct_str` shortens the oracle distance by only `{python} RackEndVerification.oracle_cut_pct_str`, because the diminished traction cancels out the majority of the kinematic savings.

**Result**: F1 passes only if powered deceleration begins within `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` and the base travels at most `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` from the last valid renewal, `{python} RackEndVerification.ref_gap_str` less than the capture-referenced subtotal.

**Systems insight**: Both formulations share the identical deceleration trajectory $\ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection)$; they diverge entirely on their reference event. The design subtotal incorporates `{python} RackEndVerification.age_travel_str` of evidence-age travel alongside the localization bound and protective margin that protect a detected target. However, a stalled proposer produces no target. If the verification harness evaluated an F1 proposer stall against this generous capture-referenced subtotal, the distance predicate would tolerate a braking onset roughly `{python} RackEndVerification.late_equiv_str` late, more than double the entire onset deadline. Verifying the fundamental invariant $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ remains sound only when travel is measured strictly from the physical or temporal event that the fault disrupts.

:::

The partial budget beneath both bounds reproduces the arithmetic of the design record, serving as a conditional oracle specification rather than empirical timing closure. A physical trial must directly instrument and log successful admission timestamps, continuing evidence age, and physical deceleration onset. Nominal proposer loop cadences cannot guarantee that lease renewals succeed before the deadline expires. Because a safety lease begins strictly upon successful admission, the renewal verification campaign must qualify the maximum inter-admission interval demanded by the lease rule (@eq-nervous-lease-rule) under realistic compute contention, bus saturation, and rejected proposals, rather than simply measuring unvetted proposer dispatch timestamps.

Both oracle bounds also assume that the safety permission pipeline, required perception channels, and powered traction drives survive the injected fault. Capacitive hold-up for logic rails and brake coils cannot sustain the traction drives during heavy braking. The power-loss fallback (F4b) must therefore maintain and monitor a verified auxiliary power reserve and dynamic braking dissipation path throughout deceleration. If an injected fault disables these electrical reserves, the system drops into an unpowered fallback mode whose stopping envelope must be characterized independently. Neither oracle bound relies on corrective action from either learned proposer. When the chunk policy stalls, it cannot delay braking onset: the hardware safety monitor issues the stop when the lease timer expires, with physical onset following the allocated tick, bus, and actuator path, cleanly isolating safety enforcement from proposer latency. The F1 qualification test thus benchmarks the deterministic safety permission path rather than the learned policy. Finally, this stopping budget assumes a static obstacle located at the clearance boundary. Static verification trials do not validate protection against dynamic agents moving toward the machine; site crossing restrictions and occluded-motion tracking must cover that case. Declaring these qualification points alongside both formal bounds provides the complete specification required to execute an empirical verification trial.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Tracking a moving body through occlusion, which this static-obstacle budget does not cover, is established in @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion.
:::

## One F1 Trial from Injection to Record {#sec-verification-f1-trial}

The campaign's first trial is F1, a proposer failure during transit, planned at the candidate restricted envelope point of `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str` with the full declared payload on a test floor qualified to the inspected friction. The numerical oracle remains a screening specification until loaded braking qualification supplies the actual deceleration bound. The safety claim under test is conditional. Once trajectory proposal renewals cease, the low-level permission path and motor drives must autonomously execute the resident powered stop within their allocated stopping envelope. The test deliberately halts or freezes the chunk policy immediately following its last valid lease renewal while leaving its underlying timer heartbeat active. This fault pattern cleanly separates true algorithmic progress in the proposer from the superficial liveness of an unblocked timer interrupt.

Verifying this stopping claim in its entirety requires a full physical rig: the production mobile base, motor drives, representative payload mass, and a qualified test surface. A processor-in-the-loop (PIL) bench, which runs the enforcer's compiled binary on its target microcontroller against a simulated plant, can validate lease expiration but not the plant's response, and a pure software simulation approximates both the target's execution timing and the contact mechanics. Neither bench environment alone provides empirical ground truth for physical stopping distance. Because the machine operates at the edge of its operational envelope during fault injection, an external physical containment fixture must guard the testing volume independently of whatever safety action the machine itself takes.

The temporal reference event for F1 is the last successful admission check that renewed the trajectory lease, not the upstream planner dispatch or the subsequent fault injection trigger. A complete diagnostic trace captures both the final renewal and the injection event across isolated hardware channels that independently record lease expiration, the permission path's stop command, the physical onset of powered deceleration, and external tracking of base position through complete standstill. Calibrated motor-current or torque measurements alongside wheel encoders identify drive effort and wheel response; external base-motion tracking is still needed to establish chassis deceleration under possible wheel slip. Timing uncertainty belongs in the onset margin. An auxiliary contact switch on the mechanical brake verifies subsequent holding-brake engagement. Relying on the mechanical brake switch alone would mischaracterize stopping latency, as it cannot record the initial phase of regenerative or active electric braking.

Capturing the machine's state trajectory, fault detector identity, refusal timestamp, and recovery time to a safe state demands instrumentation that is electrically and logically decoupled from the robot, such as external optical ground-truth cameras and optical shaft encoders routed to isolated digitizers. An onboard logging daemon cannot serve, because the fault under evaluation, whether a panicked kernel or a saturated interconnect bus, delays or drops the very log it would write.[^fn-probe-effect-trace] Independent external measurement helps expose false passes, where an anomalous run appears successful for reasons outside the formal safety claim. For example, injecting a dropped-frame fault might unintentionally trigger an unmonitored thermal breaker or an auxiliary ground loop that cuts drive power. If that happens, the spring-applied mechanical brake halts the base well within the distance budget, even while the software safety enforcer remains deadlocked in a priority inversion. A naive verification oracle that checks only final stopping distance would mark that trial as a success. A rigorous test harness must verify that the exact causal enforcer path specified in the safety claim commanded and governed the deceleration.

[^fn-probe-effect-trace]: **Probe Effect**\index{Probe effect!fault-injection timing}\index{Hardware tracing!CoreSight ETM}: @gait1986probe identified the probe effect in concurrent software systems, where the overhead of monitoring instrumentation alters execution timing, inadvertently masking or introducing race conditions. On-chip hardware trace units, such as Arm's CoreSight Embedded Trace Macrocell, stream cycle-accurate instruction flows over dedicated trace pins, while external protocol analyzers monitor bus transactions without altering bus arbitration. A verification trial must time the enforcer's reaction using non-intrusive hardware instruments rather than software logging daemons executing on the processor under test.

Superficial liveness signals are a second source of false passes. @Sec-nervous-supervisory-timers required that a watchdog be refreshed only when a safety-critical cycle completes, never from an independent periodic interrupt, and grounded the rule in the Toyota unintended-acceleration litigation, where expert testimony argued that a timer interrupt could keep a hardware watchdog satisfied after the control tasks had stopped [@barr2013toyota]. A design rule on paper does not show that the built machine obeys it, and F1 is the test of whether it does. The harness halts the chunk policy's task or freezes its command output while keeping the periodic interrupt handler alive (perspective \ref{psp-verification-watchdog-liveness}), and it measures the actuator response and watchdog state with external instruments. A host daemon can keep reporting a valid process heartbeat after the policy inference thread has frozen, so trial F1 passes only when physical deceleration onset is recorded at the motor drives, never on the strength of a software heartbeat logged in memory. The Toyota record adds a second question that the design rule alone does not raise, whether the supervising monitor shares an input with the processor it supervises (war story \ref{ws-verification-toyota-unintended-acceleration-limits-task-blind}).

::: {#psp-verification-watchdog-liveness .callout-perspective title="The watchdog liveness invariant"}
A watchdog serviced by a periodic timer interrupt proves only that the timer interrupt service routine executed, not that safety-critical application tasks met their deadlines, computed valid outputs, or avoided memory corruption. A qualified fault-injection campaign explicitly decouples application progress from interrupt liveness, verifying that the system initiates physical shutdown under task termination, thread starvation, and frozen control registers.
:::

::: {#ws-verification-toyota-unintended-acceleration-limits-task-blind .callout-war-story title="Testing a task-blind watchdog hypothesis"}
**Context**: In *Bookout v. Toyota* (Oklahoma County, 2013), a jury heard expert testimony on the electronic throttle control system (ETCS-i) of a 2005 Camry. The plaintiffs' software expert argued that safety-critical control tasks could fail silently while supervisory mechanisms remained blind to the failure [@barr2013toyota]. @Sec-nervous-supervisory-timers drew its watchdog rule from this testimony; the same record also bears on a second claim, the independence of the monitor that backs the watchdog.

**Mechanism**: The engine control module serviced its hardware watchdog from a recurring timer-tick interrupt rather than requiring verified progress from active control tasks. The expert testified that if the task managing throttle angle and critical fail-safes terminated due to memory corruption or a stack overflow, the throttle command could freeze at its last valid state while the timer interrupt continued to pacify the watchdog [@barr2013toyota]. The architecture included a secondary monitor processor, but testimony highlighted that this monitor could not inspect task scheduling; it could detect a dead throttle task only indirectly, through changes in brake-pedal state. A single analog-to-digital converter also digitized accelerator-pedal position for both processors, placing a common-cause failure point across the supervision boundary [@dunn2013toyota]. Recovery could therefore require the counterintuitive act of lifting a foot off the brake during the event.

**Impact**: On October 24, 2013, the jury awarded \$3 million in compensatory damages and found that Toyota had acted with reckless disregard; the parties settled before the jury could consider punitive damages [@srs2013toyota]. The verdict did not establish an uncontested technical cause. NASA's engineering review for the federal investigation found no evidence that an electronic malfunction caused large unintended accelerations [@nasa2011toyota]. It did document electronic faults, among them a tin whisker that formed a 248 Ω short within an accelerator-pedal position sensor from a 2003 Camry; vehicle tests confirmed that while this fault altered how the throttle tracked the pedal, the throttle still returned to idle whenever the pedal was released [@leidecker2011tinwhisker]. The investigation attributed the explainable incidents to floor-mat entrapment, sticking pedals, and pedal misapplication. The task-blind mechanism therefore remains an attributed hypothesis, which is exactly the kind of claim only injection can settle.

**Response**: For the design under test, fault injection must establish which application progress checks reach the watchdog, verify whether the independent monitor shares any input pathway with the processor it supervises (@sec-verification-forward-analysis), and confirm which protective inputs can reliably command a physically suitable stop. The historical controversy highlights the danger, but only direct injection testing establishes these properties for the warehouse machine.

**Systems lesson**: A periodic watchdog heartbeat confirms only that an interrupt handler continues to cycle, not that application tasks are functioning, and a monitor is independent only if no input, supply, or clock it depends on can fail together with the processor it supervises. Verification must therefore terminate the supervised task and inject faults at those shared points, measuring the actuator response with external, isolated instruments.
:::

Safety intervention mechanisms must be evaluated under the exact operational stress that makes intervention necessary. A safety enforcer that takes over cleanly on an idle development bench offers little assurance for a production vehicle. In an operational emergency, the policy model operates at maximum inference throughput, memory buses are saturated with high-resolution sensor streams, DMA controllers move camera frame buffers, and the mobile base carries its loaded rack at aisle speed. The verification framework therefore injects faults under declared worst-case thermal and electrical loads, measuring both lease-expiration revocation latency and the elapsed time between diagnostic fault assertion and powered deceleration onset at the motor drives. If the intervention path shares a system bus or memory arbiter with the neural accelerator, safety takeover can stall behind an unpreemptible burst transfer. A safety case that assumes near-instantaneous intervention without a contention bound can credit a response the deployed hardware cannot deliver.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ How a small urgent read waits behind a large burst transfer on a shared memory interconnect is established in @sec-placement-resource-contention.
:::

A verification campaign executes every injection trial under a deterministic, automated protocol, ensuring that verdicts derive strictly from repeatable physical measurements rather than post hoc interpretation. The test orchestrator first audits all operating preconditions (ambient temperature, supply rail voltages, baseline wheel speed) against declared engineering tolerances; any trial starting out of bounds aborts with a verdict of `INVALID`, which charges the failure to the fixture rather than the machine, before fault injection begins. Once preconditions hold, the orchestrator synchronizes the external plant fixture, logic analyzer, and independent ground-truth digitizers to a common reference clock, while recording the target clocks without disciplining away their injected drift. After allowing the mobile base to settle at its envelope operating point, the orchestrator asserts the fault trigger across a dedicated hardware line, registering the fault injection timestamp on the unified timeline. The isolated logic analyzer captures both this injection mark and the formal reference event (the final valid lease renewal in trial F1), so fault detection latency, drive takeover duration, and total stopping time are each scored from their true temporal origins. Concurrently, external truth sensors tied to a fail-safe crowbar relay circuit[^fn-crowbar-relay-cutoff] stand ready to initiate the test cell's qualified containment response within a measured response bound if the machine approaches its survival-envelope limit. A precommitted evaluation oracle then scores the synchronized trace against the pass/fail criteria defined in @sec-verification-oracles-acceptance; runs with corrupted or dropped external measurement frames are flagged transparently as `UNOBSERVABLE`, the verdict for a trial whose scoring telemetry was lost (@sec-verification-four-verdicts sets out all four verdicts). Finally, the test orchestrator cryptographically signs the complete trial record header and seals it into the safety evidence bundle via a cryptographic digest.

[^fn-crowbar-relay-cutoff]: **Crowbar**\index{Crowbar circuit!test containment}: The name comes from the blunt industrial act of dropping a metal bar across power supply terminals. A crowbar circuit intentionally shorts a supply rail when an overvoltage occurs, forcing an upstream fuse or breaker to trip before hazardous energy reaches sensitive loads. Within a physical fault-injection test cell, this containment concept protects physical safety at the actuator stage: independent ground-truth sensors detecting an envelope violation trigger a hardware disconnect that severs actuator drive power over a dedicated electrical pathway that the vehicle under test can neither power nor override. Physical containment therefore never depends on the correctness of the very enforcer undergoing evaluation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Protocol:** The fault-injection protocol, stage by stage with its error codes, is given in @sec-appendix-systems-fault-protocol for a reader building the test orchestrator.
:::

## Fault Oracles and Acceptance {#sec-verification-oracles-acceptance}

A valid verification trace for the F1 safety claim must establish both timely deceleration onset and bounded stopping distance; observing that the robot base eventually stopped establishes neither guarantee. Without an oracle fixed in advance, post-hoc inspection takes over: engineers eyeball time-series plots after the run, seizing on gross symptoms such as whether Joule heating\index{Joule heating!component failure} melted a motor phase wire or a controller threw an unhandled exception, and the trial degenerates into an anecdote.

::: {#dfn-verification-test-oracle .callout-definition title="Test oracle"}

***Test oracle***\index{Test oracle!definition}\index{Oracle!definition} is the predicate, fixed in full before a trial runs, that compares each independently witnessed quantity of the trace with its bound from a declared reference event and returns the trial's verdict.

1.  **Significance**: For F1, the oracle comprises two predicates evaluated from the last valid renewal: powered deceleration onset within `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` and total travel within `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` at aisle speed. Each predicate evaluates to a signed margin in its native physical unit.
