Retaining signed margins rather than binary passes enables near misses to inform subsequent trials and guides adversarial search algorithms toward razor-thin safety margins.
2.  **Distinction**: A pass criterion extracted from telemetry after a run is chosen with the outcome already visible; an oracle is mathematically precommitted. The oracle also differs fundamentally from the design budget from which it is derived: the `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` design subtotal starts at sensor capture and protects a planned target trajectory, whereas a stalled proposer produces no planned trajectory to protect.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A persistent misconception in physical verification is that a robot base stopping short of a rack signifies a passed trial. In reality, stopping within the `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clearance distance can easily conceal a safety controller that missed its deceleration deadline, or a stop triggered by an unmodeled side effect, such as a tripped thermal breaker that cut drive-bus power, rather than the deterministic safety path named in the claim.

:::

### Four-verdict test oracles and forensic integrity {#sec-verification-four-verdicts}

Rigorous verification demands an **invalid-test rule**\index{Invalid-test rule!definition} to handle runs where the test environment fails to deliver the specified physical conditions. Consider two common testbed anomalies. If traction control derates motor torque over an uneven floor seam and slows the mobile base before fault injection, the robot encounters the disturbance below its declared operating speed, invalidating the target envelope point. Conversely, if a hardware frame injector overflows its internal queue and drops an adversarial CAN message before it reaches the physical transceiver, the machine under test never encounters the disturbance. Scoring such aborted runs as passes manufactures artificial confidence; scoring them as system failures blames the vehicle for a defective test harness.

To preserve forensic integrity, the oracle returns one of four explicit verdicts: `PASS` indicates that every precommitted timing and physical predicate held under verified preconditions; `FAIL` indicates that the system violated one or more measured predicates; `INVALID` indicates that the fixture failed to establish declared test preconditions or the fault injection itself miscarried; and `UNOBSERVABLE` indicates that ground-truth telemetry required to score the trial was corrupted or lost, while the partial trace is retained for diagnosis. Under an `INVALID` or `UNOBSERVABLE` verdict, any unmeasured quantity is logged as unavailable rather than set to zero. Neither verdict may ever be converted into a `PASS`, and neither is ever omitted from aggregate coverage reports. An `UNOBSERVABLE` trial supplies no verdict on the unmeasured claim. Its missing evidence requires investigation of both the witness system and the injected fault, rather than an assumed attribution to the harness alone. Silently discarding runs with dropped telemetry or treating unobservable outcomes as passes introduces severe survivorship bias. For example, if an inductive kick from an emergency brake solenoid emits an electromagnetic interference burst that crashes the data acquisition (DAQ) logger, discarding that run directly conceals the catastrophic cyber-physical failure under test. Forensic integrity requires accounting for all four verdicts in every audit ledger.

Precommitment separates empirical evidence from post-hoc rationalization. In physical fault injection, cyber-physical interactions are noisy and counterintuitive; criteria negotiated after inspecting the trace inevitably drift to accommodate anomalous behavior. An unexpected overrun is easily dismissed as floor surface variation, or a deceleration onset that exceeds the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` bound is excused simply because the vehicle came to rest before hitting the rack.

A precommitted record locks down every physical predicate, measurement unit, normalization scale, response-time bound, and invalidation trigger before the first fault is triggered. The evaluation engine computes and logs a signed margin for each predicate, issuing a `PASS` verdict only when the declared preconditions and injection are verified, all required predicates are observable, and every timing bound and physical margin remains non-negative. If stopping distance exceeds its limit by five millimeters or powered braking begins $2\text{ ms}$ past its deadline, the record pinpoints the exact predicate that failed. Systems engineers can then use the synchronized trace to determine whether the root cause was degraded tire-floor friction, mechanical brake lag, motor thermal derating, or software diagnostic latency. Precommitment enforces Principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority} at the empirical test boundary. Because production deployment grants operational authority on the basis of these records, any verdict scored under rules relaxed after the fact would grant authority on the accident of an outcome rather than the guarantee of a verified system.

### The F1 record and its missing coverage {#sec-verification-manifest-coverage}

A **fault record**\index{Fault record!definition} cryptographically binds a finalized metadata header to the independently retained sensorimotor trace. The header formalizes the parameters shared across every execution. Identity fields specify the trial identifier and verified safety claim, the physical envelope point, the fault injection parameters (mode, magnitude, and target subsystem), and a cryptographic digest of the precommitted oracle. Outcome fields record the measured detection and takeover latencies, the signed physical margins, the four-state verdict status, a digest of the complete evidence bundle, and an asymmetric digital signature over the entire header. The high-rate, variable-length telemetry trace is archived inside the evidence bundle.

The planned F1 record at the candidate restricted envelope point, `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str` on an inspected floor with a `{python} RackEndVerification.payload_str` payload, fills these fields (@tbl-15-f1-record). As with every proposer stall, the stopping distance oracle is anchored to the timestamp of the last valid lease renewal. Under the optimistic all-weight screen on a floor with friction coefficient $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str`, @eq-verification-f1-oracle yields a stopping bound of `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_stop_bound_str` (corresponding to the sensitivity boundary in notebook \ref{nbk-verification-reference-event-gap}). This distance is strictly shorter than the `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_restricted_str` capture-referenced budget subtotal at that speed. The capture-referenced subtotal accounts for upstream sensor evidence age and fixed geometric margins while omitting dispatch-to-admission communication delay; consequently, it cannot be substituted for the renewal-referenced oracle of F1 or an end-to-end appearance-referenced bound. Of the three bounds, only the renewal-referenced one contains the complete timing path; its braking premise still awaits loaded qualification. The capture-referenced subtotal has a value but omits the dispatch-to-admission interval, and the appearance-referenced bound has no value at all, because it still lacks a witnessed appearance-to-capture interval as well as a measured dispatch-to-admission interval (@fig-15-reference-events).

::: {#fig-15-reference-events fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Three reference events, three bounds**: One stop on a time axis from capture, with the dispatch-to-admission interval drawn at the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str` that would spend the spare. That ceiling, not the `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.delta_da_str` allocation, is drawn because the interval is still unmeasured and the ceiling is the longest value any trial could accept. The renewal-referenced F1 oracle counts only the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` lease path and the stop. The capture-referenced subtotal adds the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_age_str` evidence age but not the dispatch-to-admission interval. An appearance-referenced bound would need both that interval and the unwitnessed appearance-to-capture interval, and no value for it exists yet." fig-alt="Horizontal time axis from capture, 0 to 300 milliseconds, with events marked: appearance before capture on a hatched interval labeled unmeasured and not to scale, capture at 0, dispatch at 51.6 ms with an upper value of 51.8, a red hatched dispatch-to-admission interval to the last valid renewal at about 152 ms labeled 100.8 ms spends the spare, lease expiry 60 ms later, a shaded onset allowance, and onset 82 ms after renewal, followed by a stop of 931 ms to rest at 1.3 m/s. Below, three bars: renewal-referenced, starting at the last valid renewal, 751.9 mm at 1.3 m/s and 629.6 mm at 1.0 m/s; capture-referenced, solid from capture to dispatch, dotted across the dispatch-to-admission interval, then solid, 969.0 mm at 1.3 m/s and 831.2 mm at 1.0 m/s; and appearance-referenced, starting with a hatched segment at appearance, labeled as needing a witnessed appearance-to-capture interval and a dispatch-to-admission bound, with no value yet."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THREE REFERENCE EVENTS FOR ONE STOP (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-15-reference-events
# │ Goal:    show which intervals the renewal-, capture-, and appearance-referenced
# │          bounds include
# │ Show:    capture, dispatch at 51.6 ms, dispatch-to-admission drawn at the 100.8 ms
# │          that spends the spare, last valid renewal, expiry, onset; bounds
# │          751.9/629.6 mm (renewal) and 969.0/831.2 mm (capture)
# │ How:     event times and bounds from RackEndVerification
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_stop_time

R = RackEndVerification

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t_age = R.t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude  # category: derived
t_upper = R.upper_age.to(millisecond).magnitude  # category: derived
t_da_max = R.t_spare.to(millisecond).magnitude  # category: derived (Delta_da that spends the spare)
t_lease = R.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude
t_tick = R.t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude
t_bus = R.t_bus.to(millisecond).magnitude
t_act = R.t_act.to(millisecond).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t_renew = t_age + t_da_max  # admission drawn at the latest point that keeps the spare
t_exp = t_renew + t_lease
t_onset = t_exp + t_tick + t_bus + t_act
T_stop = calc_scurve_stop_time(R.v_aisle, R.a_brake, R.j_brake).to(millisecond).magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs((t_onset - t_renew) - R.onset_bound.magnitude) < 1e-9, "Renewal to onset is the 82 ms oracle bound.")
check(abs(t_age + R.onset_bound.magnitude - R.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-6, "Age plus onset bound is tau_delay.")
check(abs(t_renew - 152.375) < 1e-3 and abs(t_onset - 234.375) < 1e-3, "Capture-to-admission 152.4 ms and capture-to-onset 234.4 ms maxima.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
ink, soft, bad = C["primary"], "#4A5568", C["RedLine"]
c_ren, c_cap, c_app = C["GreenLine"], C["BlueLine"], C["VioletLine"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
x0, x_app, x_end = -62, -48, 300
y_ev = 3.2

# event line
ax.plot([-6, x_end], [y_ev, y_ev], color=ink, lw=1.2, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("", xy=(x_end + 8, y_ev), xytext=(x_end - 2, y_ev), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=ink, lw=1.2))
# appearance-to-capture interval: unmeasured, drawn without a scale
ax.fill_between([x_app, -2], y_ev - 0.12, y_ev + 0.12, facecolor="white", edgecolor=soft, hatch="////", lw=0.8, zorder=2)
ax.text((x_app - 2) / 2, y_ev - 0.22, "unmeasured,\nnot to scale", fontsize=7, color=soft, ha="center", va="top")
# Delta_da interval, drawn at the ceiling that spends the spare
ax.fill_between([t_age, t_renew], y_ev - 0.12, y_ev + 0.12, facecolor=C["RedL"], edgecolor=bad, hatch="\\\\\\\\", lw=0.8, zorder=2)
ax.text(
    (t_age + t_renew) / 2,
    y_ev - 0.22,
    f"$\\Delta_{{\\mathrm{{da}}}}$: outside the subtotal;\n{t_da_max:.1f} ms spends the spare",
    fontsize=7,
    color=bad,
    ha="center",
    va="top",
)
# onset allowance
ax.fill_between([t_exp + t_tick + t_bus, t_onset], y_ev - 0.12, y_ev + 0.12, color=C["GreenL"], lw=0, zorder=2)

events = [
    (x_app, "appearance", "D", c_app, True),
    (0.0, "capture", "o", c_cap, True),
    (t_age, f"dispatch\n{t_age:.1f} ms (≤ {t_upper:.1f})", "|", ink, False),
    (t_renew, "last valid\nrenewal", "s", c_ren, True),
    (t_exp, f"expiry\n+{t_lease:.0f}", "|", ink, False),
    (t_onset, f"onset\n+{R.onset_bound.magnitude:.0f}", "|", ink, False),
]
for x, lab, m, col, ref in events:
    if ref:
        ax.plot([x], [y_ev], marker=m, ms=8, color=col, zorder=5, mec="white", mew=0.8)
        ax.text(x, y_ev + 0.28, lab, fontsize=8, color=col, ha="center", va="bottom", fontweight="bold")
    else:
        ax.plot([x, x], [y_ev - 0.14, y_ev + 0.14], color=ink, lw=1.2, zorder=4)
        ax.text(x, y_ev + 0.28, lab, fontsize=7.5, color=ink, ha="center", va="bottom")
ax.text(x_end + 4, y_ev + 0.28, f"stop at {R.v_aisle.magnitude:.1f} m/s:\n{T_stop:.0f} ms to rest", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, ha="right", va="bottom")

def bracket(y, segs, col, label, hatch=None):
    for a, b, solid in segs:
        if solid:
            ax.plot([a, b], [y, y], color=col, lw=4.0, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.plot([a, b], [y, y], color=col, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1.5, 2)), zorder=3)
    if hatch:
        a, b = hatch
        ax.fill_between([a, b], y - 0.07, y + 0.07, facecolor="white", edgecolor=col, hatch="////", lw=0.8, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x_end + 8, y), xytext=(x_end - 2, y), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=col, lw=1.2))
    ax.text(x0 + 2, y + 0.16, label, fontsize=7.8, color=col, ha="left", va="bottom")

y1, y2, y3 = 2.05, 1.2, 0.35
bracket(
    y1,
    [(t_renew, x_end, True)],
    c_ren,
    f"renewal-referenced (F1 oracle): {R.onset_bound.magnitude:.0f} ms, then the stop; "
    f"{R.f1_aisle_stop_bound.magnitude:.1f} mm at {R.v_aisle.magnitude:.1f} m/s, "
    f"{R.f1_stop_bound.magnitude:.1f} mm at {R.v_restricted.magnitude:.1f} m/s",
)
bracket(
    y2,
    [(0, t_age, True), (t_age, t_renew, False), (t_renew, x_end, True)],
    c_cap,
    f"capture-referenced (budget subtotal): {R.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude:.1f} ms, then the stop; "
    f"{R.budget.magnitude:.1f} mm at {R.v_aisle.magnitude:.1f} m/s, "
    f"{R.budget_restricted.magnitude:.1f} mm at {R.v_restricted.magnitude:.1f} m/s",
)
bracket(
    y3,
    [(-2, x_end, True)],
    c_app,
    "appearance-referenced: needs a witnessed appearance-to-capture interval and a $\\Delta_{\\mathrm{da}}$ bound; no value yet",
    hatch=(x_app, -2),
)
ax.plot([x_app, x_app], [y3 - 0.07, y3 + 0.07], color=c_app, lw=1.0)

ax.set_xlim(x0, x_end + 12)
ax.set_ylim(0.05, 4.05)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks([0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300])
ax.set_xlabel("time after capture (ms); the stop continues beyond the axis", fontsize=9)
ax.grid(False)
for s in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_bounds(0, x_end)
plt.show()
```

:::

In the planned record (@tbl-15-f1-record), the outcome field contains no numerical value and is marked unavailable. Because no physical trials have been executed in this book, the field specifies the physical measurement that will eventually populate it; until empirical data are recorded and verified by independent witnesses, the record remains uncommitted and carries no verdict. The trial count in that field is a design choice of its own. The number of passing trials needed to bound the miss probability follows the zero-failure count of @sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim, which @sec-verification-campaign-statistics applies to an injected fault population.

| Trial and claim                                                                                | Envelope point                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Oracle, predeclared from the last valid renewal                                                                                                        | Detector and witness                                                                             | Outcome to be measured                                                                                                 | Verdict                                                                                                     |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| F1, proposer stall: chunk-policy task killed one tick after a renewal; rack-end stopping claim | `{python} RackEndVerification.v_restricted_str`; `{python} RackEndVerification.payload_str` payload; test floor measured at $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str`; drive bus at `{python} RackEndVerification.bus_nominal_str` nominal | Powered deceleration onset $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str`; travel to rest $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_stop_bound_str` | Lease timer on the permission path; expiry, revocation, and onset each on its own wire and clock | Trial count; maximum onset and maximum travel over the trials, each with its signed margin; unavailable until measured | None until scored; `PASS` requires verified preconditions, required witnesses, and both nonnegative margins |

: **One F1 fault record at the candidate restricted envelope point**: The header fields of a proposer-stall trial on the warehouse mobile manipulator, with the screening oracle awaiting loaded braking qualification before the run and the outcome left as the measurement that must fill it. {#tbl-15-f1-record tbl-colwidths="[18,22,18,14,16,12]"}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The record header, field by field and including how an unavailable value is encoded, is given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-fault for a reader building the ledger.
:::

The record schema maintains strict forensic separation among verdicts on a per-field basis. If an upstream breaker trips and prevents an injection, the harness marks the run `INVALID`. For any run aborted prior to injection, the detection latency, takeover delay, and stopping margin are recorded as unavailable rather than coerced to zero. The evidence bundle attaches an explicit validity flag and missing-data reason code to each measurement. The scoring oracle inspects these validity flags before performing any statistical or arithmetic evaluation, ensuring that unmeasured fields never corrupt pass-rate calculations, latency percentiles, or margin statistics.

A single aggregate percentage conceals where the verification campaign never ventured. A system that survives 98 percent of five thousand fault injection trials demonstrates remarkably little if every trial ran at nominal room temperature under negligible memory bus contention. Comprehensive verification requires reporting coverage across orthogonal dimensions: functional safety claims, physical envelope extremes, physical and logical injection sites, timing distribution tails, hardware build revisions, and concurrent multi-fault scenarios. For the warehouse mobile manipulator, physical envelope coverage verifies whether faults were injected under both empty and fully loaded rack states, at nominal aisle speed on dry concrete, at restricted speed on inspected surfaces, and under depleted DC drive-bus voltages. Timing tail coverage isolates injections scheduled to coincide with p99 operating system scheduling jitter in the permission loop or saturated DMA bus traffic. System verification cannot be declared complete when an aggregate coverage score exceeds a target percentage; rather, the minimum coverage across every individual dimension must satisfy the safety case requirements.[^fn-std-iso-injection]

[^fn-std-iso-injection]: **Scope of assurance standards**\index{ISO 26262!Hardware Fault Injection}: ISO 26262-5 addresses road-vehicle electrical and electronic hardware. Its single-point and latent fault metrics concern the architecture and its allocated safety goals; they are not the failure-rate-weighted aggregate coverage against which notebook \ref{nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time} later sizes an injection campaign. Fault injection is one way to test diagnostic assumptions, alongside analysis and other evidence. ANSI/UL 4600 frames an autonomous-vehicle safety case from multiple kinds of evidence. Neither standard makes a fixed number of hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) trials sufficient for release.

Repeated trials provide statistical evidence only when underlying physical or digital states vary. Executing a deterministic fault script five hundred times on a digital bench with identical initial register states, fixed clock dividers, and synchronized inputs traverses the exact same execution path on every iteration; it contributes no more statistical information than a single run. Conversely, on a physical test aisle, repetition samples real-world stochasticity: micro-variations in wheel-floor contact friction, asynchronous hardware interrupt arrivals, bus arbitration jitter, and phase drift between the camera exposure clock and the policy inference cycle. In that setting, repeated trials characterize the variance and map the dangerous tails of the end-to-end response-time distribution.

::: {#chk-verification-oracles-verdicts .callout-checkpoint title="Oracles, verdicts, and reference events"}

An F1 result carries meaning only through the oracle, reference event, and verdict rule fixed before the run.

**Scoring a trial**

- [ ] **Verdict assignment**: Can you score three trials, one in which the injector dropped the fault packet before it reached the transceiver, one in which the logger crashed while the base stopped short of the rack, and one in which every predicate held on independent witnesses, and name the record fields each trial leaves unavailable?
- [ ] **Reference event**: Can you explain why the F1 distance oracle starts at the last valid renewal and leaves out the evidence age and the two margins that the capture-referenced subtotal carries?
- [ ] **Repetition vs. variation**: Can you explain why five hundred runs of a deterministic bench script count as one trial, while repeated runs on the test aisle sample a distribution?

**Estimating a margin**

- [ ] **Onset estimate**: A trial at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` records powered deceleration onset `{python} RackEndVerification.chk_onset_str` after the last valid renewal, with the lease expiring and the stop command issuing on time. Can you estimate the onset margin, the extra travel before braking begins, and whether the trial can pass even though the base stops well short of the rack?

:::

## Extending the Trial to the Envelope {#sec-verification-extending-trial}

The F1 record fixes one trial at one envelope point, and even a clean pass there says nothing about the points around it. The operating-envelope definition already warned that the danger lies at coupled corners, where two parameters that are each within their declared ranges combine to break the claim. Extending the trial therefore means choosing which further points to test, and that choice follows from how the machine's physics couples its variables.

### Multi-dimensional boundary coupling vs. scalar sweeps {#sec-verification-boundary-coupling}

For an embodied system such as a mobile manipulator, specifying independent minimum and maximum thresholds for individual operating variables fails to capture the true operational boundary. Physical mechanics, compute pipeline latency, and electrical power distribution interact dynamically. Sweeping a single parameter in isolation while holding all other variables at nominal levels leaves the dangerous coupled corners of the operational envelope completely untested:

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_floor_friction_ceiling_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Optimistic all-weight screening curve of the speed ceiling against floor friction: flat at 1.44 meters per second for friction above 0.204, falling below it to 1.23 meters per second at a friction of 0.12. A dashed horizontal line at the 1.3 meters per second aisle speed turns red, over a shaded region, where it lies above the curve."}

*The `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed clears the dry-floor ceiling but not the inspected floor's.*
:::

- **Surface friction and travel speed**: The `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed and an inspected floor friction of `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` each fall well within their declared individual operating ranges. In combination, however, they fail even the optimistic all-weight traction screen. On low-friction surfaces, the tire-floor interface, not mechanical braking capacity, sets an upper limit on deceleration; in the all-weight screen it falls to `{python} RackEndVerification.a_insp_str`. Consequently, the resident stopping maneuver elongates: the required stopping distance at `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` expands to `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_insp_str`, exceeding the available `{python} RackEndVerification.d_clear_str` clearance. The optimistic screening ceiling on that floor drops to `{python} RackEndVerification.ceiling_insp_str`, and the actual speed limit must use the qualified loaded lower bound rather than assuming this ceiling is attainable.
- **Contact nonlinearities and dynamic load transfer**: Real warehouse floors rarely exhibit an idealized, static friction coefficient $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$. Instead, surface friction varies dynamically based on local contamination (such as concrete dust, ambient moisture, or oil films), wheel tread heating, and transient wheel loading. On the running machine only the two driven hub wheels brake against the floor, so the traction ceiling is $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \Gravity \DrivenWheelLoadFraction$, where $\DrivenWheelLoadFraction$ is the share of the weight those wheels carry (derived in the free-body diagram of @sec-body, @fig-02-braking-fbd). During hard braking, the inertial load $\Mass\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ acting at the center of gravity pitches the body forward and can move normal force off the driven wheels onto the front caster, lowering $\DrivenWheelLoadFraction$ exactly when traction is needed. If the drives demand braking torque sized for the static load share, the driven wheels slip and the net braking force collapses. Under a constant-friction approximation, the braking distance then grows as $\SpeedAtDetection^2 / (2\CoulombFrictionCoefficient \Gravity \DrivenWheelLoadFraction)$, inversely with the friction actually delivered at the driven wheels and quadratically with speed.
- **Computational and electrical coupling**: Memory and power subsystems couple directly into safety margins. A compute-heavy forward pass of the vision-language-action intent model executing on the application SoC can saturate unified memory bandwidth. This contention delays camera-buffer processing and postpones the compact evidence handoff to the safety microcontroller, inflating the observation age and, with it, the pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$. Because stopping distance scales linearly with total reaction delay (@eq-body-stopping-distance), a `{python} RackEndVerification.late_onset_str` memory stall consumes `{python} RackEndVerification.late_extra_str` of physical clearance at aisle speed. On the electrical bus, the dominant transient coupling originates from the motor drive actuators rather than the neural compute accelerator. At its maximum `{python} RackEndVerification.soc_power_str` draw, the SoC pulls approximately `{python} RackEndVerification.soc_current_str` from a depleted battery bus, only `{python} RackEndVerification.soc_share_pct_str` of the overall `{python} RackEndVerification.i_rail_str` transient, whereas the two drive motors demand up to `{python} RackEndVerification.drive_peak_str` during peak torque transients. Severe acceleration can sag the common DC bus across battery internal resistance and wiring harness impedance, while bursty inference activity primarily stresses the SoC's local point-of-load regulators, a localized transient that the F4 campaign must isolate and measure separately.
- **Payload mass and kinematic posture**: Arm posture and payload distribution couple directly to stopping performance through vehicle stability and load transfer. Under braking, the base tips about its front caster whenever deceleration exceeds $\Gravity\,\LeadingSupportDistance/\GravityCenterHeight$, where $\GravityCenterHeight$ is the height of the center of gravity and $\LeadingSupportDistance$ its distance behind that caster; this is the tip-over ceiling of notebook \ref{nbk-body-braking-drive-limits}, which the credible deceleration respects only while $\GravityCenterHeight/\LeadingSupportDistance$ stays below the ratio computed there. Raising the arm above a storage rack raises $\GravityCenterHeight$, and reaching forward shortens $\LeadingSupportDistance$, so posture moves the machine toward that ceiling. The tip-over threshold can bind before tire traction saturates, and ISO 3691-4 mandates physical stability verification for driverless industrial trucks [@iso3691part4]. Unloaded trials support only their tested configurations; they cannot establish the fully loaded deceleration or the complete operating envelope. That notebook left both lengths unmeasured, so the envelope cannot yet certify that the demanded deceleration stays below the tipping threshold; a tilt-table test or multi-axis corner-scale measurement of the fully loaded machine must supply them.
- **Thermal throttling and fallback execution**: Sustained thermal stress can induce dynamic processor throttling, delaying action proposal generation and degrading mission throughput. In an architecture protected by an independent, verified resident stop, a missed watchdog renewal safely triggers a bounded, fail-safe stopping trajectory rather than indefinitely expanding stopping delay. Nevertheless, multi-axis compound verification must ensure that simultaneous bus contention, sensor packet drops, or voltage droops do not compromise that fallback routine itself.

### Physical perturbations vs. digital adversarial noise {#sec-verification-physical-perturbations}

Digital adversarial perturbations and physical disturbances challenge an embodied system at entirely different interfaces. Injecting synthetic pixel perturbations directly into an input tensor isolates model vulnerability; it measures how susceptible a neural network's decision boundary is to small numerical variations in representation space. However, such digital tests completely bypass the physical transduction pipeline. An optical disturbance, by contrast, exercises the physical lens, optical coatings, automated exposure and gain control, sensor demosaicing, and camera interface timing. Neither testing modality substitutes for the other. A comprehensive threat model must therefore explicitly delineate whether an adversarial fault corrupts in-flight digital packets, manipulates the external physical environment, or perturbs both interfaces simultaneously.

Evaluating the rack-end safety claim requires injecting realistic physical disturbances: stray illumination and direct glare that blind camera sensors, mechanical chassis vibration that corrupts inertial measurements, and floor transitions that slash available braking traction. Every physical injection requires a repeatable physical actuator and an independent ground-truth witness. For instance, glare injection requires calibrated illumination measurements beside the lens together with the declared optical geometry, spectrum, and temporal waveform, chassis vibration requires external optical motion capture independent of onboard wheel odometry, and floor variations require standardized friction-measurement drag sleds. In cyber-physical verification, receiving a syntactically valid sensor packet with correct checksums over an internal bus confirms only that the digital transmission succeeded; it provides no guarantee that the estimated state accurately reflects physical reality.

### What the envelope claim leaves open {#sec-verification-falsification-formulation}

Boundary testing systematically searches for counterexamples to declared safety claims. For claim F1, the initial diagnostic experiment requires no complex numerical optimization: simply suppress trajectory renewal while the base is in motion, and independently measure the deceleration-onset timestamp with its uncertainty bound and the physical position where the base comes to rest. Subsequent falsification campaigns systematically vary initial robot velocities, arm configurations, and injection phase timings to expose minimal operating margins (@sec-verification-falsification-trajectory-formulation). Formal methods, high-fidelity simulation, and physical hardware testing provide complementary evidence; none can compensate for an unstated physical premise or an unverified operating assumption.

An operating boundary remains defensible only when every parameter carries its physical unit, traceable provenance, calibrated uncertainty, and designated engineering owner. Specifying a credible deceleration of `{python} RackEndVerification.a_brake_str` remains an incomplete assertion until the verification ledger explicitly documents its origin: whether it was measured during physical stopping trials at maximum payload mass, extracted from an actuator manufacturer's datasheet, or computed using a theoretical friction model, alongside the measurement uncertainty of the external tracking reference. Any hardware modification, whether a new polyurethane wheel tread compound or new motor-drive firmware pushed across the EtherCAT fieldbus, obligates the component owner to re-evaluate whether the operational boundary has shifted.

Validating an operating envelope requires rigorously attacking its boundary surfaces rather than testing comfortable interior states. Evaluating an unloaded base crawling across a dry floor with pristine camera frames proves only that nominal execution functions under ideal conditions. Instead, the verification harness distributes test points across three critical regimes: points *just inside* the envelope verify that the control policy preserves closed-loop stability\index{Closed-loop stability} under the largest permissible operational stress; points *on the boundary* confirm that safety margins survive nominal sensor noise and compute jitter; and points *just outside* verify that the safety enforcer reliably preempts the policy, executing a deterministic stop that halts the base within the survival envelope before clearance is exhausted.

A physical hardware malfunction and an algorithmic functional insufficiency require fundamentally different verification strategies. A stereo camera can reliably transmit uncorrupted, perfectly timed video packets over PCIe while ambient glare completely blinds its depth perception algorithms. A complete verification campaign must therefore inject faults into both the physical execution mechanisms and the sensory information streams upon which those mechanisms rely. Simply assigning an enforcer module does not magically grant it observability over physically unobservable conditions; when physical sensing cannot distinguish safe states from hazardous ones, the system architect must restrict the operational envelope to a domain where safety can be enforced.

::: {#psp-verification-hardware-falsification .callout-perspective title="The hardware falsification principle"}
A hardware-dependent safety claim needs an observable challenge to its physical premises\index{Fault injection!hardware}. If the campaign cannot inject the relevant disturbance or retain the required witness, the record must preserve that verification gap.
:::

Once every timing constraint, latency budget, and environmental threshold is quantitatively specified, the design claims established throughout this book become concrete targets for fault injection\index{Fault injection}, each paired with an explicit boundary threshold that must trigger protective intervention\index{Protective intervention}.

## Deriving the Fault List {#sec-verification-deriving-fault-list}

The proposer stall fault (F1) originates from negating a fundamental operational claim: that proposal renewal proceeds reliably within its granted lease. Deriving a comprehensive fault list, however, requires two complementary methodologies. Inverting design records tests the explicit assumptions codified across the system architecture. Working forward from the physical realities of mechanics, power networks, and human interaction exposes the hazards and unmodeled edge cases that software design records routinely omit.

### Inverting design records and the five-element chain {#sec-verification-inverting-records}

The first source of faults is the design records, inverted. @Sec-data through @sec-evaluation state the learned policy's properties: its training distribution, its state-action assumptions, and its inference latency ceilings. @Sec-perception through @sec-placement establish interface and execution properties such as bus allocations, observation freshness, and estimation bounds, while @sec-intervention defines how quickly authority transfers away from a failing policy and which subsystem holds the override. If the machine's specification asserts that the chunk policy renews its trajectory proposal every `{python} RackEndVerification.chunk_period_str` at every speed up to the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_drive_str` drive limit, the verification suite inverts that claim. The test environment injects stalled renewals, delayed observations, and out-of-range encoder readings to verify whether the permission path detects the violation within its allocated latency budget.

The five-part test contract of @sec-verification-fault-injection states what makes any trial valid evidence. A second list of five, which also opens with a claim and closes with an oracle, states how one fault is built into such a trial. Its first element supplies the contract's bounded claim, its last element supplies the contract's oracle, and the three between them are the mechanism the trial exercises. For every candidate fault, the bounded claim and its injection procedure form this **five-element chain**:

1. **The negated condition:** the exact architectural or timing invariant violated (for example, proposal renewal halted after lease issue);
2. **The physical injection point:** the exact hardware or bus interface where the disturbance enters (for example, an inline field-programmable gate array (FPGA) serializer, CAN FD disturbance node, or programmable DC load);
3. **The expected detector:** the deterministic monitoring primitive tasked with catching the violation (for example, a lease countdown timer or evidence-epoch comparator);
4. **The bounded response:** the deterministic transition executed by the enforcer (for example, revoking proposal authority and commanding the resident stop suffix); and
5. **The observable pass condition:** the quantitative, independently witnessed metric that scores the trial (for F1 at aisle speed, onset $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` and travel from renewal $\le$ `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str`).

A recorded design property becomes a testable fault only when all five elements are fully defined and observable. If any element of this chain cannot be defined or measured, the architecture exhibits a **verification gap**\index{Verification gap!definition}. A verification gap reveals that the underlying claim cannot be falsified by empirical test. Systems engineers cannot ignore such gaps; resolving them requires dedicated hardware instrumentation (such as external optical trackers or non-intrusive trace macros), a narrower operational design domain, or a structural redesign of the execution path.

Inversion also applies to the learned proposer's implicit assumptions, where distribution shift can induce functional insufficiency even when every observation frame arrives intact and on time. For example, a chunk policy trained in simulation on dry concrete with friction coefficient `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_dry_str` proposes decelerations that an inspected floor at `{python} RackEndVerification.mu_insp_str` turns into wheel slip. Inverting that evaluation claim requires injecting degraded traction conditions at the physical contact patch. Sensor bias, calibration drift, and input perturbations are injected for the same reason: a policy exhibiting high nominal reward can still command high-frequency actuator chatter once its inputs deviate from nominal distributions. Under these conditions, an overly permissive execution path can destabilize the plant while executing syntactically valid commands, demonstrating that software commands and mechanical dynamics remain tightly coupled across the causal boundary.

At each inter-module contract, the fault list negates architectural guarantees directly at their physical handoff points: observation freshness, state validity, intent lifetime, planning deadlines, enforcement independence, and resource allocation. For the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_lease_str` chunk lease, the test harness replays the expired admitted record `{python} RackEndVerification.lease_probe_at_str` after its last valid renewal, verifying that the permission path firmly refuses to extend execution authority. A concurrent proposal represents an entirely separate admission attempt: it must satisfy fresh evidence, kinematic state validity, mode consistency, and stopping-reserve checks before receiving a lease. To test the enforcer's claimed independence from the policy processor on the selected discrete placement, the verification suite saturates the application processor's memory interconnect with DMA traffic while independently timing the safety microcontroller. Host contention may delay proposal delivery and age its supporting evidence, but the enforcer must still satisfy its `{python} RackEndVerification.enforcer_deadline_str` execution deadline within every `{python} RackEndVerification.t_tick_str` control tick. This rigorous inversion prevents arbitrary over-testing: bus contention, clock skew, and supply fluctuations are injected precisely where the architecture claims tolerance, rather than drawing from generic fault menus that impose requirements the machine was never specified to meet.

Inversion exhibits an inherent structural limit: it only surfaces faults originating in assumptions the design team explicitly modeled. The resulting fault list is therefore only as comprehensive as the recorded architectural claims. If no engineering record documents how the base's spring-applied brake behaves when its friction lining glazes under repeated emergency stops, inversion cannot synthesize the failure mode, and the hazard never reaches the test suite.

### Forward physical analysis and common-cause modes {#sec-verification-forward-analysis}

A second, independent source works forward from the physical machine, enumerating what the mechanical body, the power distribution network, the floor interface, and the operational environment can produce regardless of software state. Drive wheels skid when commanded deceleration exceeds the traction limit of the contact patch; brake linings glaze under repeated thermal cycles; solid tires wear down, altering the rolling radius that wheel odometry relies on; and structural vibration gradually loosens camera mountings until spatial calibration drifts. These hazards originate in contact mechanics, thermal dynamics, and tribology, physical domains that no software abstraction represents. Nancy Leveson's **Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP)**\index{Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes!definition} framework[^fn-std-stpa-leveson] [@leveson2011engineering] provides the systems foundation for incorporating these emergent physical phenomena into hazard analysis.

[^fn-std-stpa-leveson]: **STAMP and STPA**\index{Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis!emergent hazards}: @leveson2004new proposed STAMP, which treats safety as a dynamic control problem rather than a component-reliability problem, recognizing that catastrophic accidents often arise from unsafe interactions among components that each operate strictly within specification. @leveson2011engineering established the Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) hazard-analysis method on this foundation, identifying unsafe control actions at subsystem interfaces, such as an integration seam where bus communication latency or digital filter lag erodes phase margin. Because no individual component has failed at such a seam, its unsafe control actions supply critical fault modes that inverting nominal design records cannot expose.

Consider a motor drive that continues producing positive torque after receiving a stop command. A shorted inverter switch, welded contactor, or stuck gate-driver enable line can defeat the normal powered stopping trajectory. The test harness must independently observe delivered phase torque, rotor velocity, and the engagement of the secondary isolation path. While Safe Torque Off (STO) inhibits torque generation without providing electrical isolation, it cannot enforce nominal stopping distances on low-friction floors or prevent back-driving on gravity-loaded articulated joints. The safety architecture must specify a separately justified containment response alongside an independent physical measurement oracle. If no such path exists, the fault exposes a fundamental architectural omission rather than an operational delay that can borrow from the normal stopping budget.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Safe Torque Off and the industrial stop categories are established in @sec-enforcement-stop-categories.
:::

Working forward exposes hardware fault classes that software design records rarely imply: loss of reference clocks, power supply brownouts that leave digital logic in indeterminate voltage states, pulse-width modulation (PWM) inverter switching noise coupling into differential encoder lines, corrupted non-volatile configuration registers, and reset lines that bridge domains intended to remain galvanically or logically isolated. For instance, if the safety microcontroller and the high-performance application processor share a single power-management integrated circuit (PMIC), a transient voltage droop during a sudden drive-current surge can reset both processors simultaneously just as the learned proposer loses trajectory tracking. A software interface model that assumes an ideal DC power supply omits this failure. An enforcer cannot arrest an errant policy if it loses operating power alongside the workload it supervises; the deterministic safety runtime must outlive the faulted workload using independently qualified execution and power resources. The running machine uses an isolated, capacitor-backed auxiliary supply to survive the declared supply fault.

Forward physical analysis likewise evaluates the architecture's common-cause independence claims. Subsystems that appear strictly isolated on an architectural block diagram frequently share physical vulnerabilities. For example, the primary lidar communication lines and redundant safety bumper wiring may share a single mechanical cable carrier subject to pinch wear, depend on a shared analog voltage reference inside a multichannel converter, or rely on timer silicon containing identical silicon errata. An electrical transient that latches up both channels simultaneously destroys any safety argument predicated on statistical independence. **Common-cause analysis**\index{Common-cause analysis!definition} traces harness routing, power distribution paths, and clock distribution trees to identify shared failure paths and justify independence against the declared fault set, rather than assume separation from the block diagram.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The independence claims for the permission path's execution unit, oscillator, power rail, and memory are established in @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation.
:::

This physical analysis extends directly to human error and foreseeable operational misuse. Warehouse personnel may jumper an optical rack-end sensor during maintenance, leave a manual pallet jack parked across an automated transit corridor, or unplug an acoustic warning beacon to silence workplace noise, while remote teleoperators may request transit speeds exceeding local aisle restrictions. When a remote assistant commands the vehicle's full `{python} RackEndVerification.v_drive_str` drive limit within a narrow aisle, the verification suite must confirm that the arbiter denies the command by capability constraint or clamps it to the admitted manual mode speed under an active `manual_drive` state. Furthermore, the deterministic permission check must evaluate the assistant's command with the same scrutiny applied to autonomous proposals.

Working forward from the physical plant adds a representative mechanical failure mode, the actuator jam, to the record-derived inventory in @tbl-15-fault-classification. Achieving verification completeness still requires a plant-specific hazard analysis tailored to the vehicle's mechanical kinematics and operational envelope.

In addition to inverted design claims and forward physical hazards, the fault suite must systematically evaluate the four authority transition cases (A1–A4) established in @sec-intervention-evidence-tuples. Each case occupies a dedicated row in @tbl-15-fault-classification and must be evaluated under the operating state that makes intervention most urgent: a fully loaded base approaching the rack end at velocity. The test campaign injects takeover requests at two speeds to distinguish the candidate moving transition from a request the clearance screen rejects; the operative design stops before handing over. At the `{python} RackEndVerification.v_takeover_str` slow-down, the partial-budget waiting margin is `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_takeover_str`, enough for the `{python} RackEndVerification.t_takeover_str` in-loop takeover and the `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.delta_da_str` dispatch-to-admission allocation together, so @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines identifies a candidate moving in-loop handover for qualification, subject to the complete session ledger and live stopping checks; the trial must show that a handover left pending still ends in a local stop by its deadline. At the full `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` aisle speed the margin is `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, only `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.t_left_str` once the allocation is charged, which cannot hold the takeover, so the arbiter must reject the moving handover and dispatch a local stop before the deadline expires. An out-of-loop takeover begins only after a stop, from standstill, in an admitted mode. Evaluating either sequence solely while the vehicle is parked proves nothing about dynamic performance; the trial must demonstrate that rejection, timeout, and braking occur with bounded latency while the base moves.
