```{python}
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.6), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.45, 1.0], "hspace": 0.42})

ink, soft, ok, bad = C["primary"], "#4A5568", C["GreenLine"], C["RedLine"]
rows = [
    ("proposer renewals", "task log + trigger line"),
    ("chunk lease", "permission-path timer"),
    ("stop command", "logic analyzer"),
    ("drive frame", "fieldbus sniffer"),
    ("powered deceleration", "drive current + encoder"),
]
ys = [4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
H = 0.55
xmax = 130
for (name, witness), y in zip(rows, ys):
    ax.axhline(y, color=C["grid"], lw=0.6, zorder=1)

def step(y, t_on, hi_first, color, **kw):
    lo, hi = y, y + H
    if hi_first:
        xs, yy = [0, t_on, t_on, xmax], [hi, hi, lo, lo]
    else:
        xs, yy = [0, t_on, t_on, xmax], [lo, lo, hi, hi]
    ax.plot(xs, yy, color=color, lw=1.6, zorder=4, **kw)

# proposer: last valid renewal pulse at 0, task killed at 1 ms, probe refused at 65 ms
ax.plot([0, 0, 1.2, 1.2, xmax], [4, 4 + H, 4 + H, 4, 4], color=ink, lw=1.6, zorder=4)
ax.plot([1.2], [4 + H + 0.12], marker="x", color=bad, ms=6, mew=1.6, zorder=5)
ax.text(3.0, 4 + H + 0.12, "task killed", fontsize=7.5, color=bad, va="center")
ax.plot([t_probe, t_probe], [4, 4 + H * 0.7], color=soft, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=4)
ax.text(t_probe - 1.5, 4 + H * 0.45, f"probe proposal at {t_probe:.0f} ms, refused", fontsize=7.5, color=soft, va="center", ha="right")
# lease valid until expiry
step(3, t_lease, True, ink)
ax.text(t_lease + 1.5, 3 + H + 0.08, f"expires {t_lease:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
step(2, t_cmd, False, ink)
ax.text(t_cmd + 1.5, 2 + H + 0.08, f"next tick {t_cmd:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
step(1, t_frame, False, ink)
ax.text(t_frame + 1.5, 1 + H + 0.08, f"bus {t_frame:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
# onset allowance window and the two onsets
ax.fill_between([t_frame, t_onset], -0.15, H + 0.15, color=C["GreenL"], alpha=0.8, zorder=0, lw=0)
ax.text((t_frame + t_onset) / 2, H + 0.2, "onset\nallowance", fontsize=7.0, color=ok, ha="center", va="bottom")
ax.axvline(t_onset, color=ok, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.plot([0, t_onset, t_onset, xmax], [0, 0, H, H], color=ok, lw=1.8, zorder=5, label="onset at the bound")
ax.plot([0, t_late, t_late, xmax], [0, 0, H, H], color=bad, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=5, label="late-onset example")
ax.annotate("", xy=(t_late, -0.32), xytext=(t_onset, -0.32), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=bad, lw=1.0))
ax.text((t_onset + t_late) / 2, -0.42, f"onset margin $\\rho$ = \u2212{t_late - t_onset:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=bad, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(t_onset - 1.5, 4.95, f"onset bound {t_onset:.0f} ms", fontsize=7.5, color=ok, ha="right", va="bottom")

ax.set_yticks([y + H / 2 for y in ys])
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{n}\n({w})" for n, w in rows], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlim(-3, xmax)
ax.set_ylim(-0.95, 5.25)
ax.set_xticks(range(0, xmax + 1, 10))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("time after the last valid renewal (ms)", fontsize=9)
ax.grid(False)
for s in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)

# speed panel
bx.axvspan(0, xmax, color=C["grid"], alpha=0.25, lw=0, zorder=0)
bx.text(xmax / 2, 0.08, f"0 to {xmax} ms,\npanel above", fontsize=7.0, color=soft, ha="center", va="bottom")
bx.plot(t, v_bound, color=ok, lw=1.8, zorder=4)
bx.plot(t, v_late, color=bad, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=4)
end_b = t_onset + T_stop * 1000
end_l = t_late + T_stop * 1000
bx.text(
    end_b - 30,
    0.52,
    f"rest at {end_b:,.0f} ms\ntravel {R.travel_nominal.magnitude:.1f} mm\n{R.eps_track.magnitude:.0f} mm allowance remains",
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=ok,
    ha="right",
    va="center",
)
bx.text(
    end_l + 25,
    0.36,
    f"rest at {end_l:,.0f} ms\ntravel {R.travel_late.magnitude:.1f} mm\n$\\rho$ = {R.rho_dist.magnitude:+.0f} mm",
    fontsize=7.5,
    color=bad,
    ha="left",
    va="center",
)
bx.set_xlim(-3, 1250)
bx.set_ylim(0, v0 * 1.18)
bx.set_xlabel("time after the last valid renewal (ms)", fontsize=9)
bx.set_ylabel("base speed (m/s)", fontsize=9)
bx.tick_params(labelsize=8)
bx.text(8, v0 + 0.05, f"{v0:.1f} m/s aisle speed", fontsize=7.5, color=ink, va="bottom")
for s in ("top", "right"):
    bx.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

:::

Recording every monitored channel on one timeline, as illustrated in @fig-15-hardware-fault-injection, helps localize a failed trial to a stage of the response path when the independent witnesses remain valid. A lease that expires on schedule and a stop command issued at the very next tick, followed by a late braking onset, direct the investigation toward command delivery, drive execution, or physical brake response rather than the lease-expiry check.

By producing a continuous, signed margin rather than a binary pass/fail flag, quantitative robustness transforms verification from passive testing into **temporal logic falsification as adversarial optimization**\index{Temporal logic falsification!definition}. In classical computer vision and deep learning, adversarial attacks such as the fast gradient sign method (FGSM) [@goodfellow2015explaining] and projected gradient descent (PGD) [@madry2018towards] search for an input perturbation $\AdversarialPerturbation$ bounded within an $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$-ball ($\|\AdversarialPerturbation\|_\infty \le \AdversarialPerturbationBudget$) that maximizes task loss: $\max_{\|\AdversarialPerturbation\|_\infty \le \AdversarialPerturbationBudget} \LossFunction(\ParameterizedPredictor(\ModelInput + \AdversarialPerturbation), \ExampleLabel)$. In cyber-physical systems, temporal logic falsification provides the continuous dynamic counterpart. Rather than perturbing static feature vectors, an adversarial optimizer searches over initial state spaces and time-varying physical disturbance trajectories within a bounded physical disturbance envelope to minimize quantitative Signal Temporal Logic robustness. The robustness metric $\StlRobustness$ acts directly as the adversarial objective function.

Uniform random sampling across a high-dimensional operational state space requires an intractable number of physical trials to expose rare corner-case collisions. In contrast, an adversarial falsification engine actively steers disturbance sequences toward trajectories that drive the system closest to violating its safety invariants.

### Formulating falsification as trajectory optimization {#sec-verification-falsification-trajectory-formulation}

Formally, let $\MechanicalPlantState_0 \in \FalsificationInitialStateSet$ represent the machine's initial state vector (translational speed, payload mass, heading angle, and battery state-of-charge), and let $\DisturbanceTrajectory(\TimeInstant) \in \AdmissibleDisturbanceSet$ denote an adversarial disturbance trajectory spanning the test horizon $[0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]$. In embodied physical systems, $\DisturbanceTrajectory(\TimeInstant)$ cannot be an unconstrained, discontinuous mathematical function: physical actuators, real sensors, and contact surfaces exhibit finite bandwidth, mechanical inertia, and thermal limits. Disturbance trajectories are therefore parameterized over a compact parameter space $\DisturbanceParameterVector \in \DisturbanceParameterSet$ using smooth basis functions, such as B-splines, cubic splines, or Fourier series:
$$\DisturbanceTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \DisturbanceParameterVector) = \sum_{k=1}^{\DisturbanceBasisCount} \DisturbanceBasisCoefficient_k \DisturbanceBasisFunction_k(\TimeInstant)$$
where $\DisturbanceBasisFunction_k(\TimeInstant)$ are time-dependent basis functions and $\DisturbanceBasisCoefficient_k$ are bounded parameter coefficients.

The temporal logic falsification problem is formulated as finding the worst-case parameter combination that minimizes quantitative robustness:
$$\min_{\MechanicalPlantState_0 \in \FalsificationInitialStateSet, \, \DisturbanceParameterVector \in \DisturbanceParameterSet} \StlRobustness(\StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory(\MechanicalPlantState_0, \DisturbanceTrajectory(\DisturbanceParameterVector)), 0) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\DisturbanceTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \DisturbanceParameterVector)\|_\infty \le \DisturbanceBudget, \quad \forall \TimeInstant \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon].$$ {#eq-verification-adversarial-falsification}

The disturbance budget $\DisturbanceBudget$ in @eq-verification-adversarial-falsification constrains the peak magnitude of optical, acoustic, contact, and execution disturbances derived from the operational envelope. However, magnitude constraints alone do not ensure physical realizability. The choice of basis functions, coefficient bounds, and experimental test fixtures must also respect realistic rates of change and duration limits. For example, a programmable load bank that cannot replicate a steep simulated voltage transient leaves that synthesized counterexample untested on hardware.

A rigorous verification campaign must log both the synthesized disturbance command and its independently measured physical realization. If the experimental fixture fails to deliver the precommitted disturbance trajectory within specified tolerances, the trial is invalid for that test condition even if the machine comes to a safe stop. While an empirically realized counterexample conclusively refutes a safety claim, a successful search across a restricted parameter family leaves arbitrary disturbances outside that chosen basis open to question.

### Selecting a search method {#sec-verification-optimization-engines}

Frictional contact transitions and discrete controller state jumps often render the quantitative robustness landscape nonsmooth and non-convex, limiting the reliability of gradient descent without additional treatment of those transitions. Derivative-free optimization methods are therefore well suited to this domain. The Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) [@hansen2001completely] dynamically updates a multivariate normal distribution over disturbance parameters, efficiently discovering correlated failure modes across speed, surface friction, and execution timing. When physical trials dominate the cost, because each execution incurs mechanical resets, inspection, and thermal cool-down, Bayesian optimization[^fn-bayesian-optimization-surrogate] balances exploration and exploitation by fitting a probabilistic surrogate model across previous runs. Neither method guarantees convergence to a global minimum over a finite campaign. The verification record must preserve search parameter bounds, random seeds, evaluated test vectors, and fixture constraints so that external auditors can reconstruct precisely what regions were challenged.

[^fn-bayesian-optimization-surrogate]: **Bayesian Optimization**\index{Bayesian optimization!expensive trials}: Originally developed for computationally expensive engineering simulations, Bayesian optimization fits a Gaussian-process surrogate across completed trials and selects subsequent sample points by maximizing expected improvement [@jones1998efficient]. Physical fault-injection rigs share these operational economics, as each trial incurs mechanical resets, hardware inspection, and thermal stabilization delays. However, the surrogate's confidence remains a model prediction: a region it estimates to be safe has not been physically tested merely because the surrogate predicts a positive margin.

Two established software toolboxes operationalize this search loop for cyber-physical models: S-TaLiRo [@annpureddy2011staliro] and Breach [@donze2010breach]. Both frameworks ingest a formal Signal Temporal Logic requirement and a simulation model, calculate quantitative robustness on each simulated rollout, and steer stochastic or local optimizers toward negative robustness. A related family of algorithms treats the disturbance sequence itself as a sequential decision process. **Adaptive stress testing**\index{Adaptive stress testing} [@lee2020adaptive] explores the disturbance sequence via Monte Carlo tree search or reinforcement learning to discover the most probable path to failure rather than an arbitrary, physically improbable edge case, thereby ranking counterexamples by operational plausibility. A comprehensive taxonomy of these black-box methods organizes them by their output [@corso2021survey]: discovering an isolated counterexample, finding the most likely failure trajectory, or estimating an aggregate failure probability. Only the third outcome provides a valid measure of operational risk, an estimation process detailed in @sec-verification-importance-sampling.

Search algorithms return candidate counterexamples and measured robustness margins. When a candidate failure originates in simulation, incorporating it into a physical safety claim requires an exact accounting of the discrepancy between modeled dynamics and real-world trajectories.

### Sim-to-real transfer validation and discrepancy bounds {#sec-verification-sim-to-real-bounds}

In physical AI systems, high-throughput software-in-the-loop simulation is indispensable for exploring combinatorial corner cases, but an unvalidated simulator can only confirm what its underlying model already assumes. The cure for the digital twin delusion is a number, the bound on how far the simulator's trajectories may stray from the machine's. To use simulation sweeps as valid evidentiary warrants in a structured safety case, the engineering team must formally validate and bound the **sim-to-real transfer gap** $\TransferDiscrepancyBound$\index{Sim-to-real transfer gap!discrepancy bounds}\index{Simulation-to-reality leap!validation bounds}.

Let $\SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \SimulationParameterVector, \ControlInput) \in \TrajectoryStateSpace$ and $\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant; \SimulationParameterVector, \ControlInput) \in \TrajectoryStateSpace$ denote the system state trajectories in simulation and on target physical hardware under matched declared conditions $\SimulationParameterVector$ (initial speed, payload mass, floor friction) and control input history $\ControlInput$. Replaying identical open-loop input sequences establishes a baseline comparison of plant dynamics. However, certifying a deployed closed-loop policy requires bounding discrepancy under autonomous execution, where perturbed sensor observations induce divergent actuator commands; an open-loop replay bound alone cannot establish closed-loop validity. The continuous transfer discrepancy is defined as the supremum state error across the test horizon $[0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]$ under a task-weighted physical norm:
$$\TransferDiscrepancyBound = \sup_{t \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]} \|\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant) - \SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)\|_{\StateNormWeighting}$$ {#eq-verification-sim2real-gap}
where $\|\cdot\|_{\StateNormWeighting}$ normalizes position, velocity, and actuator torque errors by predeclared positive reference scales in meters, meters per second, and newton-meters, respectively, before applying dimensionless task weights. The verification ledger fixes those scales and weights; the resulting discrepancy $\TransferDiscrepancyBound$ is dimensionless, while the Lipschitz constant $\PredicateLipschitzConstant$ carries the physical units of the predicate margin.

Establishing a rigorous safety warrant requires a discrepancy bound that holds across all trajectories in the claimed operational envelope, rather than merely recording the largest error observed in a finite test sample. The allowable modeling error must be deducted directly from the simulated robustness margin. Consider a Signal Temporal Logic safety requirement $\StlFormula$ whose atomic predicates $\StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) \ge 0$ are Lipschitz continuous with constant $\PredicateLipschitzConstant = \sup_{\SignalTrajectory_1 \ne \SignalTrajectory_2} |\StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory_1) - \StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory_2)| / \|\SignalTrajectory_1 - \SignalTrajectory_2\|_{\StateNormWeighting}$. Here $\PredicateLipschitzConstant$ represents the maximum rate at which the predicate margin degrades per unit of normalized state discrepancy; for a spatial clearance predicate evaluated in meters against position error normalized by a 1 m reference scale with unit task weight, $\PredicateLipschitzConstant$ is 1 m per unit of normalized discrepancy. By Lipschitz continuity, the physical predicate error is bounded pointwise by the state discrepancy:
$$|\StlPredicateFunction(\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) - \StlPredicateFunction(\SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant))| \le \PredicateLipschitzConstant \|\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant) - \SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)\|_{\StateNormWeighting} \le \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound$$
which guarantees that at every instant $\TimeInstant \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]$:
$$\StlPredicateFunction(\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) \ge \StlPredicateFunction(\SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) - \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound.$$
Taking the infimum across the temporal horizon $\TimeInstant \in [0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]$ for an invariance property $\StlFormula \equiv \square_{[0, \FiniteTimeHorizon]} (\StlPredicateFunction(\SignalTrajectory(\TimeInstant)) \ge 0)$, the guaranteed lower bound on physical robustness in the real world is:
$$\PhysicalStlRobustness \ge \SimulatedStlRobustness - \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound.$$ {#eq-verification-robustness-discount}
The term $\PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound$ in @eq-verification-robustness-discount acts as a **sim-to-real robustness discount**. If simulated robustness $\SimulatedStlRobustness$ does not exceed $\PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound$, the simulation pass guarantees no physical margin at all: the real machine can breach the safe invariant set ($\PhysicalStlRobustness < 0$) even when every simulated rollout returns a positive margin.

The rack-end claim makes this discount concrete. Scoring the distance predicate in meters and normalizing position error by a 1 m reference scale with unit task weight gives a Lipschitz constant of 1 m per unit of normalized discrepancy. Suppose a simulated stop finishes with the entire `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` reserve intact. The lower bound in @eq-verification-robustness-discount certifies a positive physical margin when $\TransferDiscrepancyBound <$ `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_gap_max_str`, meaning the justified position-error bound is smaller than the reserve under this normalization. A larger discrepancy bound leaves the actual physical margin unresolved. A simulator whose stopping position is experimentally validated to within a few centimeters transfers nearly all of its verified margin; a simulator that has never been calibrated against physical stopping runs transfers none of it.

Coupled cyber-physical dynamics determine the phenomena this discount must cover: drivetrain compliance and gear backlash alter delivered torque, surface contamination and tire wear change braking traction, and real-time execution jitter alters braking onset time. A discrepancy bound calibrated on an unloaded, cool machine cannot be silently extended to a loaded vehicle operating under thermal throttling. The verification record must explicitly define the operational envelope across which the discrepancy bound is justified, strictly separating that theoretical bound from the empirical maximum error observed during paired test runs.

Empirical measurement of $\EmpiricalTransferDiscrepancy$ builds on the paired probing protocols used to qualify simulation models for policy training, driving identical command histories into both simulated and physical hardware while scoring channel residuals against precommitted tolerances (@sec-training-contact-exploit). Verification adapts this qualification procedure with two key modifications. First, excitation inputs are tailored directly to the specific safety invariant under test, such as full-rate deceleration from aisle speed for the rack-end claim rather than low-speed docking maneuvers. Second, physical trajectories must be captured with external instrumentation independent of the robot's onboard sensor suite, ensuring that shared sensor calibration errors or estimator drift cannot cancel out of the residual. The resulting empirical discrepancy $\EmpiricalTransferDiscrepancy$ is archived in the test records alongside the environmental conditions under which it was gathered. If the sim-to-real safety case relies on domain randomization distributions $\DomainRandomizationDistribution$ to envelop hardware variations, it must justify set inclusion across all declared operational conditions:
$$\PhysicalTrajectorySet(\SimulationParameterVector) \subseteq \bigcup_{\SampledSimulationParameterVector \sim \DomainRandomizationDistribution} \SimulatedTrajectorySet(\SampledSimulationParameterVector).$$
While finite paired measurements can falsify this inclusion by exposing an outlier, they cannot establish it globally. If unmodeled physical effects such as fieldbus latency jitter, magnetic stator saturation, transmission backlash, or Coulomb stiction cause physical trajectories to escape the randomized simulation bundle, the sim-to-real transfer guarantee becomes void, and software-in-the-loop simulation passes cannot serve as evidentiary warrants in the release safety case.

::: {#chk-verification-temporal-logic-oracles-and-falsification .callout-checkpoint title="Search, robustness, and transfer"}

A signed margin turns testing into search, and a simulated margin counts toward a physical claim only after its transfer discount.

- [ ] **Quantitative robustness interpretation**: Can you explain how Signal Temporal Logic replaces binary pass/fail assertions with a signed predicate margin, and how its units and reference limit determine the meaning of a negative score?
- [ ] **Adversarial optimization of disturbance trajectories**: Can you describe how black-box optimizers use quantitative robustness scores to discover worst-case combinations of latency, noise, and friction?
- [ ] **Test invalidation vs. failure criteria**: Can you distinguish between an execution that falsifies a safety invariant and an invalid trial where testbed preconditions or fault injection mechanisms failed?
- [ ] **Normalization scale estimate**: For the late F1 trace of @sec-verification-stl-robustness, suppose the record had fixed the distance scale at the `{python} RackEndVerification.eps_track_str` tracking inset while keeping the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` onset scale. Can you estimate both normalized margins and say whether the governing predicate changes for this trace?
- [ ] **Transfer discount**: A simulated F1 stop keeps `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` of reserve. Can you state the largest discrepancy bound that still guarantees a positive physical margin, and explain why a bound measured on an unloaded, cool machine cannot certify a loaded, throttled one?

:::

## Interpreting Campaign Statistics {#sec-verification-campaign-statistics}

Tabulating the results of adversarial test trials does not immediately yield an estimate of operational risk. Any statistical summary describes only the specific population sampled by the test harness, and tests that were never conducted remain missing evidence regardless of how sophisticated the subsequent analysis becomes.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-injected-population-trials
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ZERO-MISS INJECTION COUNTS FOR A SAMPLED FAULT POPULATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: fault-manifest section and @nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time.
# │ Show: Zero-miss injections needed to put a one-sided upper limit on the miss probability,
# │       and the coverage (98.98 and 99.90 percent) and injection counts (293 and 2,935)
# │       that the notebook's illustrative FIT rates and chosen targets imply.
# │ How: n = ceil(ln(1 - C) / ln(1 - p)), the zero-failure sizing of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_zero_failure_sample_size
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_percent, fmt_int, fmt_display_math, check

class InjectedPopulationTrials:
    """Zero-miss injection counts for a declared fault population."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen
    # Component fault rates for the coverage notebook, in FIT (faults per 1e9 h)
    fit_sensors = 1500  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_compute = 1000  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_power = 2500  # transceivers and power management; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_gate = 4800  # gate drivers; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    fit_target_1 = 100  # unmitigated-rate target; category: chosen
    fit_target_2 = 10  # tighter unmitigated-rate target; category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    fit_raw = fit_sensors + fit_compute + fit_power + fit_gate
    c_diag_1 = 1.0 - fit_target_1 / fit_raw  # required coverage: lambda_raw (1 - C) <= target
    c_diag_2 = 1.0 - fit_target_2 / fit_raw
    # Injections that demonstrate each coverage: miss probability p = 1 - C_diag
    n_cov_1 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(c_diag_1, confidence=confidence)
    n_cov_2 = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(c_diag_2, confidence=confidence)
    n_cov_1_exact = math.log(1.0 - confidence) / math.log(c_diag_1)
    rule3_1 = 3.0 * fit_raw / fit_target_1  # the rule-of-three approximation 3/p
    rule3_2 = 3.0 * fit_raw / fit_target_2

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(fit_raw == 9800, "Component fault rates must sum to 9,800 FIT")
    check(c_diag_1 < c_diag_2 < 1.0, "A tighter target must need more coverage")
    check(n_cov_1 == 293 and n_cov_2 == 2935, "Coverage counts drifted from 293 and 2,935.")
    check(abs(n_cov_1 - rule3_1) < 2 and abs(n_cov_2 - rule3_2) < 6, "The counts sit within a few injections of 3/p.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, style="prose")
    fit_sensors_str = fmt_int(fit_sensors, commas=True)
    fit_compute_str = fmt_int(fit_compute, commas=True)
    fit_power_str = fmt_int(fit_power, commas=True)
    fit_gate_str = fmt_int(fit_gate, commas=True)
    fit_target_1_str = fmt_int(fit_target_1)
    fit_target_2_str = fmt_int(fit_target_2)
    c_diag_1_pct2_str = fmt_percent(c_diag_1, precision=2, style="prose")
    c_diag_2_pct2_str = fmt_percent(c_diag_2, precision=2, style="prose")
    n_cov_1_str = fmt_int(n_cov_1, commas=True)
    n_cov_2_str = fmt_int(n_cov_2, commas=True)
    rule3_2_str = fmt_int(round(rule3_2), commas=True)
    raw_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\lambda_{{\text{{raw}}}} = {fit_sensors} + {fit_compute} + {fit_power} + {fit_gate} = {fit_raw}\ \text{{FIT}}, \qquad"
        rf" C_{{\text{{diag}}}} \ge 1 - \frac{{\lambda_{{\text{{target}}}}}}{{\lambda_{{\text{{raw}}}}}} = 1 - \frac{{{fit_target_1}}}{{{fit_raw}}} = {fmt(c_diag_1, precision=4)}"
    )
    count_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"n \ge \frac{{\ln(1 - C)}}{{\ln C_{{\text{{diag}}}}}} = \frac{{\ln {fmt(1.0 - confidence, precision=2)}}}{{\ln {fmt(c_diag_1, precision=4)}}}"
        rf" = {fmt(n_cov_1_exact, precision=1)} \;\Rightarrow\; n = {n_cov_1}, \qquad \frac{{3}}{{p}} = \frac{{3 \lambda_{{\text{{raw}}}}}}{{\lambda_{{\text{{target}}}}}} = \frac{{3 \times {fit_raw}}}{{{fit_target_1}}} = {round(rule3_1)}"
    )
```

When $\ZeroFailureTrialCount$ independent Bernoulli trials sampled from the declared fault distribution yield zero missed mitigations, the outcome establishes a one-sided upper confidence limit on the miss probability for that specific distribution. This sample sizing directly mirrors the zero-failure trial sizing developed in @sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim, applied here to an injected hardware fault population rather than closed-loop policy rollouts. Formally, observing zero misses bounds the miss probability below $\TrialFailureProbability$ at confidence level $\ConfidenceLevel$ once $(1-\TrialFailureProbability)^{\ZeroFailureTrialCount} \le 1 - \ConfidenceLevel$. At a `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.confidence_pct_str` confidence level, this bound requires approximately $3/\TrialFailureProbability$ consecutive successful injections. To translate these injection counts into a hardware coverage claim weighted by each component's failure rate in FIT (failures in time, one per $10^9$ operating hours; notebook \ref{nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time} gives the component weights $\ComponentFailureRate_i$), the injection harness must sample faults in direct proportion to their raw failure rates $\ComponentFailureRate_i$, or the verification pipeline must apply an explicitly justified stratified weighting across each fault stratum.[^fn-math-zero-failure]

[^fn-math-zero-failure]: **Trial sampling and aging**\index{Zero-failure testing!independence}: The binomial count assumes independent, identically distributed Bernoulli outcomes under the declared injection distribution; it does not require Poisson event arrivals. Repeated heating, mechanical wear, or contact changes can violate independence, demanding a state-stratified experimental design.

This statistical bound holds only when the empirical injection outcomes satisfy the declared independence and sampling assumptions. In real hardware, repeated high-energy stops induce Joule heating ($\WindingCurrent^2\ElectricalResistance$)\index{Joule heating!fault coupling} in the drive motor windings and mechanical brake linings. This thermal buildup alters winding resistance and lining friction coefficients, coupling successive trials. Consequently, a test campaign executed on a dry aisle at room temperature cannot establish a valid confidence bound for an inspected floor or for the operating envelope's `{python} RackEndVerification.ambient_lo_str` thermal extreme.

The notebook below draws its rates from four component strata (sensors, compute, transceivers and power management, gate drivers), and each stratum maps onto rows of @tbl-15-fault-classification. Sensor faults are injected as F2 and as the physical transducer disturbances, compute faults as F1, transceiver and power-management faults as F3 and F4, and gate-driver faults as the drive that keeps producing torque after a stop command (@sec-verification-forward-analysis). Sampling in proportion to the rates therefore fixes how the campaign's trials divide among those rows.

::: {#nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time .callout-notebook title="The coverage count"}

**Problem**: Illustrative component fault rates and a chosen ceiling on the unmitigated rate fix the diagnostic coverage the machine needs. How many zero-miss injections, sampled in proportion to those rates, would demonstrate that coverage?

**Variables**:

* Component fault rates $\ComponentFailureRate_i$ in FIT, one fault per $10^9$ operating hours (Illustrative): sensors `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_sensors_str`, compute `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_compute_str`, transceivers and power management `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_power_str`, and gate drivers `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_gate_str`.
* Target unmitigated rate $\TargetHazardRate =$ `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_1_str` FIT, with a stricter `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_2_str` FIT alternative, at confidence $\ConfidenceLevel =$ `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.confidence_pct_str` (Chosen).
* Diagnostic coverage $\DiagnosticCoverage$, the $\ComponentFailureRate_i$-weighted fraction of faults whose hazardous effect is mitigated, so that $\UnmitigatedHardwareFaultRate = \RawHardwareFaultRate(1 - \DiagnosticCoverage)$ and a single injection misses with probability $\TrialFailureProbability = 1 - \DiagnosticCoverage$.

**Math**:

*Required coverage.*
`{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.raw_math`

*Injections to demonstrate it*, from the zero-failure count of @sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim.
`{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.count_math`

*Sensitivity.* The count scales as $3\RawHardwareFaultRate/\TargetHazardRate$, so the `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_2_str` FIT target needs `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.c_diag_2_pct2_str` coverage and `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.n_cov_2_str` injections, against a rule-of-three estimate of `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.rule3_2_str`.

**Result**: A `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.fit_target_1_str` FIT target needs `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.c_diag_1_pct2_str` coverage, which `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.n_cov_1_str` zero-miss injections demonstrate at `{python} InjectedPopulationTrials.confidence_pct_str` confidence.

**Systems insight**: The target unmitigated failure rate, not the number of entries in the fault list, governs campaign size. Every tenfold tightening of the target rate demands roughly a tenfold increase in physical injection runs. Furthermore, this sample size is valid only when injections are drawn strictly in proportion to each component's raw failure rate $\ComponentFailureRate_i$. Injecting uniformly across components with disparate failure rates evaluates a synthetic, distorted distribution unless the test harness weights the empirical outcomes and gathers sufficient evidence within every stratum. Every individual trial must therefore log the exact injected mode, whether hardware detection triggered within the deadline, and whether the safety controller brought the physical plant to a verified safe state.

:::

Accumulating passive operational fleet hours cannot compensate for gaps in the deliberate fault injection campaign. As demonstrated by the exposure wall in @sec-evaluation-limits, zero-failure operational testing cannot feasibly demonstrate the ultra-low hazard rates required for a safety certification claim. The fault-record set must therefore catalog omitted test cases as carefully as completed runs. The verification dossier must explicitly record every parameter regime bypassed due to testbed physical limits, sensor bandwidth constraints, or destructive testing costs; unprobed regions cannot be credited as verified safety margins in the release case.

### Exposure and the population a statistic describes {#sec-verification-exposure-wall}

Operational fleet exposure and targeted fault injection sample different distributions, and @eq-eval-exposure-wall already priced the first. Under a constant hazard rate, failure-free operation bounds the rate $\TargetHazardRate$ only after about $3/\TargetHazardRate$ operating hours at 95 percent confidence, the continuous-time counterpart of the rule of three for trial counts (@eq-eval-rule-of-three), and @butler1993infeasibility showed why that wall makes raw fleet hours an infeasible route to safety-critical rates such as $10^{-9}$ failures per hour. Verification adds the question of which population those hours describe. Unguided fleet mileage rarely exercises the corner-case faults this chapter injects, so operational exposure substantiates a statistical claim only when the event taxonomy, operating envelope, runtime intervention policies, and hardware-software configuration all match the deployment baseline. Any modification to a safety filter, control policy, or actuator driver may change the sampled outcomes, and earlier fleet hours count toward the new configuration only through an explicit engineering argument that the change left the counted events unaffected.

### Estimating a rare failure rate by importance sampling {#sec-verification-importance-sampling}

Adversarial falsification identifies whether an unsafe trajectory exists, but deployment and release decisions require quantifying how frequently such failures occur under nominal operating conditions. Naive Monte Carlo sampling from nominal operating profiles is computationally intractable because nearly every trajectory terminates in an unremarkable, safe stop; bounding rare failure rates through zero-failure testing demands billions of runs at the safety-critical rates of @sec-verification-exposure-wall. **Importance sampling**\index{Importance sampling!definition}[^fn-importance-sampling-shielding] resolves this computational bottleneck by generating rollouts from an alternative proposal distribution that deliberately targets the rare failure domain, subsequently applying likelihood-ratio weights to each sample to restore an unbiased estimate under the true operational distribution.

[^fn-importance-sampling-shielding]: **Importance Sampling**\index{Importance sampling!origins}: The technique originated in Monte Carlo calculations of nuclear radiation shielding during the early 1950s, where the few particles that penetrated dense shielding were exceptionally rare yet safety-critical. @kahn1953methods formalized importance sampling alongside correlated sampling and statistical estimation to drastically reduce required sample counts. However, the technique introduces a severe vulnerability: a proposal distribution that fails to cover a valid failure path will report vanishingly small sample variance and yield an erroneously optimistic failure probability, an outcome known as a support failure that diagnostic checks must detect.

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-rare-event-is
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ IMPORTANCE SAMPLING AND THE CROSS-ENTROPY METHOD ON THE RACK-END OVERSHOOT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-verification-importance-sampling.
# │ Goal: Estimate the probability that an unbudgeted queue delay exhausts the
# │       rack-end reserve, and compare plain Monte Carlo, zero-failure testing,
# │       and importance sampling with a cross-entropy proposal.
# │ Show: failure when the delay exceeds T_latest = 100.8 ms; with an
# │       exponential delay of mean 5 ms, p = 1.8e-9; plain Monte Carlo needs
# │       5.7e10 runs for 10 percent relative error, zero-failure testing 1.7e9;
# │       the cross-entropy proposal (mean 105.8 ms after 4 levels) needs about
# │       2,700 runs, within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal.
# │ How: closed forms for an exponential operational delay and an exponential
# │      proposal; the expected (large-sample) cross-entropy iteration
# │      (calc_monte_carlo_sample_size, calc_importance_sampling_exponential,
# │      calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal,
# │      calc_optimal_exponential_proposal_mean).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_zero_failure_sample_size
from mlsysim.physics import (
    calc_monte_carlo_sample_size,
    calc_importance_sampling_exponential,
    calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal,
    calc_optimal_exponential_proposal_mean,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_sci, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

class RareEventOvershoot:
    """Likelihood-ratio estimate of the rack-end reserve-exhaustion probability."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_exhaust = RackEndVerification.t_spare  # queue delay that spends the reserve (T_latest); category: derived
    d_mean = (
        5 * millisecond
    )  # mean unbudgeted queue delay per stop, exponential; scenario assumption; category: illustrative (a loaded-trial delay histogram would replace it)
    elite_share = 0.1  # cross-entropy elite fraction; category: chosen
    rel_err = 0.1  # target relative standard error of the estimate; category: chosen
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    gamma = float(t_exhaust.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    m0 = float(d_mean.to(millisecond).magnitude)
    # Cross-entropy iteration (expected, large-sample form): raise the level to the
    # (1 - elite_share) quantile of the current proposal, refit the proposal mean
    # to the likelihood-weighted elite samples, which for this family is the
    # conditional mean E_p[D | D > level] = level + m0.
    ce = calc_cross_entropy_exponential_proposal(t_exhaust, d_mean, elite_share)
    levels = [lv.to(millisecond).magnitude for lv in ce["levels"]]
    n_levels = ce["n_levels"]
    m_ce = ce["proposal_mean"].to(millisecond).magnitude
    is_ce = calc_importance_sampling_exponential(t_exhaust, d_mean, ce["proposal_mean"])
    p_true = is_ce["failure_probability"]  # P(D > T_latest) under the operational model
    n_mc = calc_monte_carlo_sample_size(p_true, rel_err)  # plain Monte Carlo runs for the target error
    n_zero = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1.0 - p_true, confidence=confidence)  # @sec-evaluation-trial-limits
    relvar_ce = is_ce["relative_variance"]  # per-sample relative variance
    n_is = relvar_ce / rel_err**2
    p_q_fail = is_ce["proposal_failure_share"]  # share of proposal draws that land in the failure set
    ess_per_draw = is_ce["ess_per_draw"]  # expected (sum w)^2 / sum w^2 per draw
    n_ess = n_is * ess_per_draw
    # Best exponential proposal (minimum second moment)
    m_opt = calc_optimal_exponential_proposal_mean(t_exhaust, d_mean)
    relvar_opt = calc_importance_sampling_exponential(t_exhaust, d_mean, m_opt)["relative_variance"]
    ce_penalty = relvar_ce / relvar_opt - 1.0
    speedup = n_mc / n_is

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(gamma - 100.775) < 5e-3, "Failure threshold is the 100.8 ms spare-exhaustion delay.")
    check(1e-9 < p_true < 1e-8, "Operational failure probability is of order 1e-9.")
    check(n_levels == 4 and abs(m_ce - (gamma + m0)) < 1e-9, "Cross-entropy reaches the threshold in four levels.")
    check(0 <= ce_penalty < 1e-3, "The cross-entropy proposal is within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal.")
    check(n_is < 1e4 < n_zero < n_mc, "Importance sampling needs orders of magnitude fewer runs.")
    check(0.3 < p_q_fail < 0.5, "Roughly two in five proposal draws land in the failure set.")
    # margin_rare_event_runs_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 5.7e10, 1.7e9, and 2,709 runs
    check(
        f"{n_mc:.1e}" == "5.7e+10" and f"{n_zero:.1e}" == "1.7e+09" and math.ceil(n_is) == 2709,
        "Runs-ladder fig-alt: 5.7e10, 1.7e9, 2,709.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    d_mean_str = fmt_latency(d_mean, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    p_true_str = fmt_sci(p_true, precision=1)
    n_mc_str = fmt_sci(n_mc, precision=1)
    n_zero_str = fmt_sci(n_zero, precision=1)
    elite_pct_str = fmt_percent(elite_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    rel_err_pct_str = fmt_percent(rel_err, precision=0, style="prose")
    level_1_str = fmt_latency(levels[0] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    level_2_str = fmt_latency(levels[1] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    level_3_str = fmt_latency(levels[2] * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    n_levels_str = fmt_int(n_levels)
    m_ce_str = fmt_latency(m_ce * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    p_q_fail_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_q_fail, precision=1, style="prose")
    relvar_ce_str = fmt(relvar_ce, precision=1)
    n_is_str = fmt_int(math.ceil(n_is), commas=True)
    n_ess_str = fmt_int(round(n_ess), commas=True)
    speedup_str = fmt_sci(speedup, precision=0)
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-verify-rare-event-charged
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RARE-EVENT THRESHOLD ONCE DELTA_DA IS CHARGED (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-verification-importance-sampling, the paragraph that sets
# │          the failure threshold.
# │ Goal: Show how much the uncharged 100.8 ms threshold flatters the failure
# │       probability: the same exponential delay model evaluated at the
# │       37.5 ms left once the dispatch-to-admission allocation is charged.
# │ Show: p = exp(-37.5/5) = 5.6e-4 against 1.8e-9, about 3e5 times larger.
# │ How: closed form P(D > t) = exp(-t / mean) for the exponential delay model
# │      of RareEventOvershoot; t from AdmissionChargeVerification.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_sci, check

class RareEventCharged:
    """The importance-sampling example's failure probability at the charged threshold."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_left = AdmissionChargeVerification.t_left  # category: derived (spare less the Delta_da allocation)
    d_mean = RareEventOvershoot.d_mean  # category: illustrative (the example's delay model)
    p_uncharged = RareEventOvershoot.p_true  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_charged = math.exp(-float((t_left / d_mean).to("dimensionless").magnitude))
    ratio = p_charged / p_uncharged

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(1e-4 < p_charged < 1e-3, "Charged-threshold failure probability is of order 1e-4.")
    check(1e5 < ratio < 1e6, "Charging Delta_da raises the failure probability by more than five orders of magnitude.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    p_charged_str = fmt_sci(p_charged, precision=1)
    ratio_str = fmt_sci(ratio, precision=0)
```

Let the operational distribution of uncertain input parameters $\UncertainScenarioParameters$ be denoted by $\OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)$, and let $\FailureRegion$ define the subset of conditions leading to a safety violation. Standard Monte Carlo estimation evaluates the failure probability $\OperationalFailureProbability = \Pr_{\OperationalScenarioDistribution}(\UncertainScenarioParameters \in \FailureRegion)$ by computing the empirical failure fraction across $\EstimatorDrawCount$ independent draws from $\OperationalScenarioDistribution$. Importance sampling instead draws samples from an engineered **proposal distribution** $\ImportanceProposalDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)$ and weights each outcome by the **likelihood ratio** $\LikelihoodRatioWeight(\UncertainScenarioParameters) = \OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)/\ImportanceProposalDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)$:
$$\ImportanceSampledFailureProbability = \frac{1}{\EstimatorDrawCount}\sum_{i=1}^{\EstimatorDrawCount} \mathbb{1}[\UncertainScenarioParameters_i \in \FailureRegion]\, \LikelihoodRatioWeight(\UncertainScenarioParameters_i), \qquad \UncertainScenarioParameters_i \sim \ImportanceProposalDistribution.$$ {#eq-verification-importance-sampling}
This estimator remains mathematically unbiased as long as $\ImportanceProposalDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters) > 0$ whenever $\OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)\mathbb{1}[\UncertainScenarioParameters \in \FailureRegion] > 0$, since the likelihood weight corrects for the shift in sampling probability [@owen2013monte]. The variance of $\ImportanceSampledFailureProbability$ depends entirely on the geometry of $\ImportanceProposalDistribution$. The theoretically optimal zero-variance proposal is the operational distribution $\OperationalScenarioDistribution$ conditioned on the failure region $\FailureRegion$ ($\ImportanceProposalDistribution^*(\UncertainScenarioParameters) = \OperationalScenarioDistribution(\UncertainScenarioParameters)\mathbb{1}[\UncertainScenarioParameters \in \FailureRegion] / \OperationalFailureProbability$). Constructing $\ImportanceProposalDistribution^*$ directly is impossible because its normalizing constant is the very quantity $\OperationalFailureProbability$ under estimation. Practical verification pipelines must therefore construct parametric approximations to $\ImportanceProposalDistribution^*$.

The **cross-entropy method**\index{Cross-entropy method} [@rubinstein2004cross] systematically discovers such an approximation within a parameterized distribution family $\ParametricProposalDistribution$ by solving a sequence of intermediate rare-event problems. Beginning with an initial proposal aligned with the operational profile ($\InitialProposalDistribution = \OperationalScenarioDistribution$), the algorithm iteratively draws a sample batch from the current proposal, evaluates the performance metric, and selects an intermediate threshold at the $(1-\EliteSampleFraction)$ quantile so that a fraction $\EliteSampleFraction$ of the batch qualifies as elite runs. The parameter vector $\ProposalParameterVector$ is then updated by maximizing the likelihood-weighted log-density of these elite samples, which minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence (a measure of how far one probability distribution lies from another) to the optimal proposal on that intermediate slice. As the threshold steps forward across iterations, the proposal gradually shifts its probability mass toward the true failure boundary. For an exponential proposal parameterized by its mean, or a fixed-variance Gaussian proposal parameterized by its mean, this update admits an exact closed form: the updated mean is the weighted empirical mean of the elite draws.

Consider this method applied to the rack-end deceleration scenario. Traveling at nominal aisle velocity, the mobile base consumes its `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` stopping reserve from @sec-verification-operating-envelope in $\FallbackDeadline =$ `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, the latest-fallback deadline of @eq-intervention-latest-fallback at aisle speed. Any unbudgeted message queue delay exceeding $\FallbackDeadline$ exhausts this safety buffer, causing the physical vehicle to breach the clearance boundary. To establish an analytical baseline, assume an illustrative operational distribution where queue delays $\MessageQueueDelay$ follow an exponential distribution with mean $\MeanMessageQueueDelay =$ `{python} RareEventOvershoot.d_mean_str` (in production verification, latency measurements gathered under the declared load must justify or replace this model). Under this formulation, the analytical failure probability is $\OperationalFailureProbability = e^{-\FallbackDeadline/\MeanMessageQueueDelay} =$ `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_true_str` per stopping event. This closed-form quantity serves as an exact ground truth against which to benchmark competing sampling estimators. The threshold is deliberately the uncharged ceiling of @sec-verification-operating-envelope, which makes the example optimistic. Charging the dispatch-to-admission allocation leaves only `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.t_left_str`, and the same delay model then gives $\OperationalFailureProbability =$ `{python} RareEventCharged.p_charged_str`, about `{python} RareEventCharged.ratio_str` times larger. The comparison below keeps the uncharged threshold because there the failure is rarest and the gap between estimators widest; at the charged threshold even plain Monte Carlo would need far fewer runs.

The sample sizing required across these estimators stems directly from the variance of sample averages. When an estimator averages $\EstimatorDrawCount$ independent draws with mean $\OperationalFailureProbability$ and per-sample variance $\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2$, the estimator's standard deviation is $\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation/\sqrt{\EstimatorDrawCount}$, yielding a relative standard error $\RelativeStandardError = \sqrt{\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2 / (\OperationalFailureProbability^2 \EstimatorDrawCount)}$. Achieving a target relative precision $\RelativeStandardError$ requires $\EstimatorDrawCount = (\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2 / \OperationalFailureProbability^2) / \RelativeStandardError^2$ trials, where $\EstimatorDrawStandardDeviation^2 / \OperationalFailureProbability^2$ denotes the per-draw **relative variance**. For naive Monte Carlo, each trial is an indicator variable with variance $\OperationalFailureProbability(1 - \OperationalFailureProbability)$, demanding approximately $(1 - \OperationalFailureProbability)/(\OperationalFailureProbability \RelativeStandardError^2)$ simulated runs. Under the illustrative delay model, securing an estimate with $\RelativeStandardError =$ `{python} RareEventOvershoot.rel_err_pct_str` relative error requires `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_mc_str` trials. By comparison, a zero-failure qualification campaign requires `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_zero_str` consecutive incident-free runs simply to establish an upper bound at the $\OperationalFailureProbability$ threshold (@eq-eval-rule-of-three).

For the exponential example, the per-draw variance equals the weighted failure indicator's second moment minus the square of the operational failure probability. The helper `calc_importance_sampling_exponential` evaluates that moment from the operational mean, proposal mean, and failure threshold and returns the relative variance used in the run count; its finite-variance condition requires the proposal rate to be less than twice the operational rate.

The cross-entropy method using exponential proposals with an elite fraction of $\EliteSampleFraction =$ `{python} RareEventOvershoot.elite_pct_str` demonstrates how adaptive sampling overcomes this barrier. The initial threshold is set at the 90th percentile of the operational delay distribution ($\MeanMessageQueueDelay\ln 10$, or `{python} RareEventOvershoot.level_1_str`). Because the exponential distribution is memoryless, the conditional distribution of delays exceeding any threshold $\CrossEntropyLevelThreshold$ is identical to the original distribution shifted by $\CrossEntropyLevelThreshold$. The likelihood-weighted mean of the elite samples is therefore simply $\CrossEntropyLevelThreshold + \MeanMessageQueueDelay$, which immediately defines the mean for the next proposal. Successive iterations lift the intermediate threshold to `{python} RareEventOvershoot.level_2_str` and `{python} RareEventOvershoot.level_3_str`. By iteration `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_levels_str`, the intermediate quantile surpasses the critical threshold, clamping the final level at $\FallbackDeadline$ with a proposal mean of `{python} RareEventOvershoot.m_ce_str`, the conditional expectation of the delay given a boundary violation. Under this adapted proposal, `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_q_fail_pct_str` of the generated rollouts land in the failure set, and their small likelihood weights scale each observed failure back to the operational probability. The resulting per-draw relative variance drops to `{python} RareEventOvershoot.relvar_ce_str`. Consequently, only `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_is_str` simulation runs are needed to reach the target `{python} RareEventOvershoot.rel_err_pct_str` relative error, a factor of `{python} RareEventOvershoot.speedup_str` fewer runs than plain Monte Carlo and within 0.1 percent of the best exponential proposal. These numerical counts derive from the assumed exponential model; testing against an empirical delay histogram will yield distinct run requirements.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_rare_event_runs_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale ladder of the runs needed to estimate one rare overshoot rate: 5.7 times 10 to the 10 for plain Monte Carlo, 1.7 times 10 to the 9 for a zero-failure campaign, and 2,709 for importance sampling with a cross-entropy proposal."}

*Weighting runs near failure cuts the runs by about `{python} RareEventOvershoot.speedup_str` times.*
:::

Two statistical diagnostics safeguard the integrity of importance sampling estimates. The first is the **effective sample size**\index{Effective sample size}, defined as $\EffectiveSampleSize = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\EstimatorDrawCount} \LikelihoodRatioWeight_i\right)^2 / \sum_{i=1}^{\EstimatorDrawCount} \LikelihoodRatioWeight_i^2$ [@owen2013monte]. This metric diagnoses concentration of the likelihood weights; it does not by itself establish the precision of the weighted failure estimate, which depends on the variance of the weighted failure indicator. For the `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_is_str` runs above, the expected effective sample size is approximately `{python} RareEventOvershoot.n_ess_str`; a degenerate value approaching 1 would warn that a few outlying weights dominate the summation, rendering the estimate unstable. The second diagnostic is distribution support and tail coverage. Omitting a subregion of $\FailureRegion$ with positive operational probability violates the support condition and biases the estimate. A proposal that retains support but samples the operational tail too rarely can instead produce unstable or infinite variance, with deceptively small observed variance in a finite run. Sample variance cannot reveal an omitted failure path that generates no samples, so the campaign must justify coverage independently of its weight diagnostics. Demonstrating the practical efficacy of this approach, @okelly2018scalable applied adaptive importance sampling to end-to-end verification of autonomous driving software stacks, demonstrating multi-order-of-magnitude computational speedups over naive Monte Carlo methods while rigorously bounding rare collision events.

This structure clarifies the critical distinction between importance sampling and adversarial falsification. While an adversarial search engine also concentrates evaluation runs near the system's safety boundaries, its underlying sampling density is uncharacterized. Because falsification runs lack explicit likelihood-ratio weights, the empirical fraction of falsification failures reveals nothing about real-world failure frequency; in the illustrative example, `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_q_fail_pct_str` of the proposal runs fail even though the modeled operational failure probability is only `{python} RareEventOvershoot.p_true_str`. A quantitative failure probability estimate belongs in an engineering safety case only when accompanied by its declared operational model $\OperationalScenarioDistribution$, proposal distribution $\ImportanceProposalDistribution$, weight trajectory, effective sample size, and confidence intervals. Such an estimate constitutes a formal statement regarding the declared operating model, rather than an unmediated physical measurement of the deployed hardware.

### Extreme value theory and heavy-tailed safety distributions {#sec-verification-extreme-value-theory}

While importance sampling estimates the occurrence rate of a binary failure condition, deployment qualification often demands bounding the physical magnitude of worst-case violations. Continuous telemetry streams provide the necessary margin signals: spatial clearance $\ClearDistance - \BaseTravelDistance(\TimeInstant)$, onset slack $\HazardOnsetBound - \HazardOnset$, and actuator torque headroom $\JointTorqueLimit - \DeliveredActuatorTorque$. Near-miss events contain rich statistical information regarding the distribution's tail, information that binary pass-fail tallies discard.

Assuming an analytically convenient tail distribution without validating that it matches the underlying physics and sampling regime is a frequent pitfall\index{Extreme Value Theory!heavy tails}. For instance, a bus latency distribution subject to sporadic arbitration contention exhibits long tails that bear no resemblance to quiet bus traffic; fitting a Gaussian distribution to nominal execution data severely underestimates such tail risk. Extreme value theory provides rigorous limiting distributions for tail behavior, but engineers must establish domain validity rather than assuming power-law characteristics or mistaking a mathematical endpoint for an inviolable physical barrier.

Extreme Value Theory (EVT)\index{Extreme Value Theory!definition}\index{Generalized Pareto Distribution!GPD} supplies foundational limiting distributions for extreme deviations, playing an analogous role for tail events to that of the central limit theorem for sample means [@coles2001introduction]. While the block-maxima formulation (yielding the Generalized Extreme Value distribution) is developed in @sec-appendix-ml-evt, cyber-physical verification primarily leverages the threshold-exceedance formulation, which retains every observation exceeding a safety margin rather than discarding non-maximal data.

1. **Peaks over threshold and the Generalized Pareto Distribution**\index{Peaks-Over-Threshold!POT}\index{Generalized Pareto Distribution!Pickands-Balkema}: Let $\TailPerformanceMetric$ denote a continuous performance metric (such as stopping-distance error), and let $\ExceedanceThreshold$ represent a sufficiently high baseline threshold. We model the exceedances $\ThresholdExcessVariable = \TailPerformanceMetric - \ExceedanceThreshold$ conditional on $\TailPerformanceMetric > \ExceedanceThreshold$. For distributions in an appropriate extreme-value domain of attraction, the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem gives an asymptotic Generalized Pareto approximation to the conditional excess distribution as $\ExceedanceThreshold$ approaches the upper endpoint. @balkema1974residual and @pickands1975statistical proved this result independently:
$$\GpdCumulativeDistribution(\EvaluatedExceedance; \GpdScaleParameter, \TailShapeParameter) = 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\TailShapeParameter \EvaluatedExceedance}{\GpdScaleParameter} \right)^{-1/\TailShapeParameter}, \quad \EvaluatedExceedance > 0,$$ {#eq-verification-gpd-distribution}
defined for scale parameter $\GpdScaleParameter > 0$ on the support $1 + \TailShapeParameter \EvaluatedExceedance/\GpdScaleParameter > 0$, with the exponential distribution recovered as the continuous limit $\TailShapeParameter \to 0$. The **shape parameter** $\TailShapeParameter$ governs tail thickness: $\TailShapeParameter > 0$ indicates a heavy, power-law tail; $\TailShapeParameter = 0$ corresponds to an exponential tail; and $\TailShapeParameter < 0$ defines a bounded tail with finite endpoint $\ExceedanceThreshold - \GpdScaleParameter/\TailShapeParameter$.

2. **Return level**: For a designated return period[^fn-return-period-flood] $\ReturnPeriodTrialCount$ calibrated to the sampling interval, the **return level** $\ReturnLevel_{\ReturnPeriodTrialCount}$\index{Return level!EVT safety bounds} represents the threshold exceeded on average once every $\ReturnPeriodTrialCount$ periods:
$$\ReturnLevel_{\ReturnPeriodTrialCount} = \ExceedanceThreshold + \frac{\GpdScaleParameter}{\TailShapeParameter} \left[ (\ReturnPeriodTrialCount \ThresholdExceedanceRate)^{\TailShapeParameter} - 1 \right]$$ {#eq-verification-evt-return-level}
where $\ThresholdExceedanceRate = \Pr(\TailPerformanceMetric > \ExceedanceThreshold) = \ThresholdExceedanceCount / \TotalExecutedTrialCount$ denotes the empirical exceedance rate across $\TotalExecutedTrialCount$ trials, with $\ReturnPeriodTrialCount$ expressed in equivalent trial counts. In this subsection $\ReturnPeriodTrialCount$ is therefore a count of trials, not the test horizon of @eq-verification-adversarial-falsification. @Eq-verification-evt-return-level holds for $\TailShapeParameter \ne 0$; its continuous limit at $\TailShapeParameter = 0$ is $\ReturnLevel_{\ReturnPeriodTrialCount} = \ExceedanceThreshold + \GpdScaleParameter\ln(\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\ThresholdExceedanceRate)$. Defining a return period in calendar operating hours requires scaling by an independently justified hourly event arrival rate under a verified temporal dependence model. The product $\ReturnPeriodTrialCount\ThresholdExceedanceRate$ is dimensionless, and valid extrapolations require evaluating return levels at or above the conditioning threshold $\ExceedanceThreshold$.

[^fn-return-period-flood]: **Return Period**\index{Return period!flood engineering}: The concept originates in civil hydrology, where a 'hundred-year flood' denotes a discharge level with a 0.01 exceedance probability in any single year [@gumbel1958statistics]. The hydrological caveat applies directly to robotics: because return levels extrapolate beyond empirical records, they remain valid only to the extent that the threshold choice and underlying sampling distribution are physically justified. Counting return periods across synthetic fault injection runs provides no operational safety assurance until the operational arrival rate per hour is rigorously established.

#### Connecting adversarial falsification to EVT tail sampling {#sec-verification-falsification-evt}

Under nominal operation, exceedances beyond a conservative margin threshold occur far too infrequently to permit empirical tail fitting; the exposure wall of @sec-verification-exposure-wall limits observation of extreme events just as severely as complete failures. Adversarial falsification circumvents this scarcity by actively concentrating rollouts near violation boundaries, solving the search problem of @eq-verification-adversarial-falsification over initial plant states and disturbance parameters. Let $\KnownComponentStopDistance$ denote the design budget at the trial speed, `{python} RackEndVerification.budget_str` at aisle speed, so that $\ClearDistance - \KnownComponentStopDistance$ is the `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str` spare. For the braking-distance overshoot metric $\TailPerformanceMetric = \StoppingDistance - \KnownComponentStopDistance$, the search populates the exceedance set
$$\ExceedanceSampleSet = \{ \ThresholdExcessVariable_i = \TailPerformanceMetric_i - \ExceedanceThreshold \mid \TailPerformanceMetric_i > \ExceedanceThreshold \}$$
with dense observations near the failure frontier. These samples, however, reflect the adversary's search policy rather than the operational environment. Fitting a Generalized Pareto Distribution directly to unweighted falsification runs models the efficiency of the optimizer, not the reliability of the physical plant. To inform operational risk, the evaluation runs must originate from a declared proposal distribution and incorporate the likelihood-ratio weights of @eq-verification-importance-sampling, ensuring that both the exceedance probability $\ThresholdExceedanceRate$ and the parameter estimation reflect weighted operational likelihoods.

A fitted shape parameter serves as an architectural diagnostic rather than a definitive safety verdict:

- **Positive shape ($\TailShapeParameter > 0$):** The fitted model extrapolates a heavy upper tail, suggesting vulnerability to extreme deviations. This mathematical fit does not establish that physical overshoots are truly unbounded, but it obligates the engineering team to verify whether threshold selection, sensor noise, or unmodeled delays justify the heavy-tailed risk profile.
- **Negative shape ($\TailShapeParameter < 0$):** The fitted distribution implies a finite modeled upper endpoint at $\ExceedanceThreshold - \GpdScaleParameter/\TailShapeParameter$. This mathematical endpoint must never be conflated with a certified hardware stop or taken as proof that a runtime safety enforcer will universally contain motion. Validating real-world containment requires auditing the enforcer's underlying dynamical assumptions and independently verifying its hardware response latencies under adversarial load.

#### Sim-to-real transfer bounds on EVT return levels {#sec-verification-evt-sim-to-real}

When high-throughput testing campaigns execute on the software-in-the-loop and processor-in-the-loop (PIL) rungs of the qualification ladder, extreme value modeling produces a simulated return level $\SimulatedReturnLevel$. As established in @sec-verification-sim-to-real-bounds, physical executions diverge from simulated trajectories by a bounded sim-to-real discrepancy $\TransferDiscrepancyBound = \sup_t \|\PhysicalStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant) - \SimulatedStateTrajectory(\TimeInstant)\|_{\StateNormWeighting}$. When simulated and physical trials describe the same operational population and the overshoot metric obeys the pathwise discrepancy bound with constant $\PredicateLipschitzConstant$, that bound also limits the corresponding physical return level (@eq-verification-evt-sim2real-bound):
$$\PhysicalReturnLevel \le \SimulatedReturnLevel + \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound.$$ {#eq-verification-evt-sim2real-bound}
To certify safe deployment for a stopping-distance claim, this expanded return level must remain within the available physical margin:
$$\SimulatedReturnLevel + \PredicateLipschitzConstant \TransferDiscrepancyBound \le \ClearDistance - \KnownComponentStopDistance.$$ {#eq-verification-evt-release-condition}

The margin inequality in @eq-verification-evt-release-condition represents a necessary sanity check rather than a standalone release criterion. Satisfying this relation requires demonstrating distributional consistency between simulation and physical testbeds, proper importance-weighting when quoting operational return periods, rigorous confidence intervals on the fitted parameters, and a transfer bound $\TransferDiscrepancyBound$ that holds across the entire operating domain. Observing a small trajectory discrepancy during a handful of bench tests does not substantiate an envelope-wide sim-to-real bound.

In the rack-end deceleration scenario, the physical safety margin is `{python} RackEndVerification.spare_str`, and only `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.spare_left_str` once the dispatch-to-admission allocation is charged, so a return level of a few centimeters, widened by a transfer bound of a few centimeters more, already consumes it. Any proposed tail bound must explicitly state its underlying sample population, proposal weights, parameter estimation uncertainties, and transfer error bounds before being evaluated against this reserve. When a fault mode (such as mode F1) contains zero measured physical trials, it provides neither an empirical tail fit nor a valid return-level estimate; a mathematically fitted distribution endpoint cannot substitute for missing physical test evidence.

Every statistical metric discussed in this section is fundamentally conditional. A zero-miss count characterizes only the declared fault injection distribution; an exposure bound reflects only the exact hardware and software configuration that accumulated operating hours; an importance-sampling estimate is valid only under its declared operational model; and an extreme value return level holds only relative to its fitted tail distribution and sim-to-real discrepancy bound. Because any of these supporting premises can fail, a rigorous verification campaign never outputs an isolated scalar margin. Instead, the verification pipeline produces fault records that bind every empirical safety margin to the physical, environmental, and statistical assumptions that justify it.

## Fault Records for Release {#sec-verification-fault-manifest}

In an adversarial verification campaign, a completed F1 trial records the entire event sequence across independent physical channels: the final proposal renewal, the watchdog lease expiration, the active braking response, and the final mechanical standstill. A raw telemetry trace stored on a testbench digitizer, however, cannot certify an autonomous machine on its own. The release authority can credit that trial only if the measured trace remains verifiably bound to the safety claim, the tested envelope point, and the exact software and hardware builds under evaluation. The fault record formalizes this contract by linking the structured test header directly to the retained evidence bundle through a cryptographic digest.

The release authority receives these claim-specific **fault records**\index{Fault record!release set} alongside the contextual coverage metrics needed to interpret their physical validity. Together, they form an auditable ledger that unites the individual fault records, qualification environments, justified sim-to-real transfer arguments, statistical tail estimates, and known coverage deficits. Rather than omitting unmeasured or inapplicable test fields, the schema marks them explicitly, preventing untested operating regimes from masquerading as verified boundaries. This fault-record set directly underpins the operational safety case for release; its schema and cryptographic signatures confer no authority beyond the empirical evidence recorded within them.

In addition to design contracts, the motion-authority cases A1–A4, and the placement allocations established during system staging, the fault records draw on two critical upstream records: the omission log of the policy manifest (@sec-training-policy-manifest) and the coverage-gap catalog of the evaluation record (@sec-evaluation-logs). These upstream artifacts explicitly catalog the operational conditions, sensor degradation regimes, and environmental disturbances that the learned policy proposer never encountered during training. By pairing the record header with its underlying evidence bundle, the fault record captures the complete operational provenance of the test: the asserted claim, physical operating point, fault injection mechanism, hardware and software revisions, raw high-speed telemetry, detection mechanisms, response latencies, physical stopping outcomes, and any secondary anomalies observed during the run.

### The fault-record set specification {#sec-verification-contract-matrix}

Every record in the fault-record set exists to support one named assurance claim $\AssuranceClaim$ within the release safety case, and its header explicitly states that claim. In the safety case structure developed in @sec-release-assurance-grammar, the top-level assurance claim $\AssuranceClaim_0$ asserts a fundamental physical invariant, such as halting within the clearance corridor ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$). That root claim decomposes into sub-claims $\AssuranceClaim_i$ governing specific operational envelopes, hardware fault categories, and fallback behaviors. The F1 records substantiate the assurance claim that the safety permission path halts the loaded mobile base within its travel bound once proposal renewals cease. The F2 and F3 records substantiate that same stopping guarantee when sensor observations arrive stale or fieldbus frames drop in transit. For power anomalies, the F4 records support the tested claim that the held-up auxiliary power rail keeps the permission path alive long enough through a primary supply collapse to complete an emergency stop and engage all mechanical holding brakes. Actuator-jam records demonstrate that the chassis remains within its designated lateral clearance corridor during a wheel-lock event without inducing stator winding thermal runaway. The A1–A4 records support the tested claims that motion authority maintains a single writer, prevents control bypass, executes deterministic fallback when supervisory handovers stall, and rejects forged command tokens. Finally, proposer-injection records show whether the tested proposals traversed the runtime permission checks. Extending that result to every proposal also requires the architectural or formal argument that no source can bypass the permission path.

A physical trace supports an assurance claim $\AssuranceClaim$ only through a structured argument. In a rack-end deceleration claim, for example, a raw brake-onset trace provides essential empirical evidence, but the engineering argument must explain why the digitizer clock synchronization, fault-injection timing, payload distribution, and floor traction conditions genuinely validate the claimed physical response. Evidence accumulation across the qualification ladder—combining formal reachability guarantees for the permission filter, bounded sim-to-real falsification campaigns, and in-situ hardware injection trials—allows each assurance claim $\AssuranceClaim$ to be supported by structured, multi-legged evidence rather than an isolated empirical trial. How claims, arguments, and evidence compose into an auditable assurance case, and the notation used to represent that hierarchy, are the subject of @sec-release-assurance-grammar.

The fault records must also distinguish three failure domains, because each addresses a different engineering question about the same physical machine. A compound case may span more than one domain:

- *Functional safety*: hardware and software component faults within the safety-related control system, such as encoder failures, dropped fieldbus frames, or auxiliary power brownouts.
- *Safety of the intended functionality* (SOTIF\index{ISO 21448!SOTIF}): hazards that emerge under nominal, fault-free hardware operation due to algorithmic insufficiencies, such as perceptual occlusions, out-of-distribution optical flare, or corner-case proposer blind spots.
- *Security*: deliberate adversarial tampering with physical sensors, communication buses, or cryptographic tokens.

The consensus engineering standards governing each subsystem of the machine, with their publication editions, are organized in the standards map of @sec-release-standards-map. Passing an adversarial fault-injection campaign does not on its own establish regulatory compliance or justify operation across unmodeled environments. Instead, the release argument evaluates precisely which claims the assembled records substantiate and where residual operational risks remain.

The individual fault records, the per-rung coverage of the qualification ladder, the empirical sim-to-real discrepancy bounds, and the extreme value theory (EVT) tail parameters assemble into one cryptographically signed set. This fault-record set is the thirteenth record in the record chain, after the authority record and before the release manifest, and it carries verification evidence to the release gate\index{Fault record!schema specification}.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The record chain, numbered from the limit record to the residual-claims register, is developed in @sec-appendix-systems-record-register.
:::

The signed fault-record set establishes the formal evidentiary boundary between adversarial testing and operational release:

1. **Upstream Custody Lineage**:
   - Consumes the **authority record** (@sec-intervention-authority-log) to verify handover deadline timers ($\HandoverTimeout$, @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines), duplicate-writer rejections (A1), and supervisory token integrity.
   - Consumes the **placement record** (@sec-placement-hardware-allocation) to verify bus contention limits, power-rail droop tolerances, and thermal dissipation thresholds.
   - Consumes the **enforcement record** and its admitted commands (@sec-enforcement-telemetry) to verify control barrier function (CBF) invariant sets, quadratic program (QP) filter execution deadlines, and fallback ladder transitions.
   - Consumes the **evaluation record** (@sec-evaluation-logs) to cross-reference offline covariate drift and simulation test catalogs against physical target-hardware executions.
