2. **Downstream Release Deliverables**:
   - Delivers to the **release manifest** and its safety case (@sec-release-safety-cases-claims) the empirical, claim-specific evidence and operational bounds required by the formal release argument.
   - Delivers to the **residual-claims register** (@sec-frontier-residual-claims-register) the explicit ledger of unverified operating regimes, test-fixture bandwidth limitations, and epistemic boundaries.

@Tbl-15-verification-matrix-contract specifies the data schema of this signed fault-record set:

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-verification-fallacies-pitfalls}

A physical machine can pass every isolated component fault test yet catastrophically fail in deployment when a shared power rail, communication bus, or reference clock couples multiple subsystems or blinds their diagnostic monitors. These failures stem from **unintended causal, electrical, and temporal coupling** across architectural boundaries. Compound verification tests catch such cross-domain hazards only when enough galvanically and logically independent instrumentation survives the fault to establish the ground-truth sequence of events.\index{Fault coupling!shared resources}

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Independent local watchdog timers guarantee end-to-end physical deadline compliance.*

A perception front-end, the chunk policy, and the safety permission monitor can each execute comfortably within their local scheduling slices while an unmonitored inter-process queue buffers stale observations between them. Local watchdog timers confirm only that isolated tasks kick their respective heartbeats within software deadlines; they reveal nothing about the total age of the physical state traversing the distributed pipeline.

Consider an asynchronous buffer that inserts delay into the machine's `{python} RackEndVerification.tau_delay_str` pre-deceleration budget. The importance-sampling example of @sec-verification-importance-sampling already priced this queue. At `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` it exhausts the spare after `{python} RackEndVerification.t_spare_str`, only `{python} RackEndVerification.queue_exhaust_pct_str` of the nominal pre-deceleration interval, and once the dispatch-to-admission allocation is charged it does so after `{python} AdmissionChargeVerification.t_left_str`. The fallacy lies in what the watchdogs report while it happens. Every task-level watchdog shows nominal health as the queue expands, because no task has missed its own slice. To detect this silent failure, verification experiments must isolate each stage of the causal chain: target appearance, optical capture, message dispatch, bus admission, lease expiration, and actuator torque onset. Without stage-by-stage timestamping, latency intervals are easily overlooked or double-counted.

**Local watchdogs verify component execution, not end-to-end physical propagation.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Enforce monotonic capture-to-torque evidence epoch timestamps across all processing nodes. Compare the sensor's physical capture timestamp directly against the safety monitor's decision tick, discarding any control proposal whose total elapsed latency exceeds the safety budget regardless of healthy local thread heartbeats.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Allowing diagnostic logging and high-throughput telemetry to share fieldbuses with real-time safety loops.*

Real-time fieldbuses in physical AI (such as CAN FD and EtherCAT) are engineered for deterministic, low-latency control: EtherCAT cyclic Process Data Objects (PDOs) and CAN FD priority-arbitrated frames carry microsecond-accurate torque targets and lease-renewal heartbeats. When engineering teams attempt to capture rich diagnostic traces by multiplexing high-throughput telemetry (diagnostic core dumps, raw LiDAR point clouds, uncompressed camera debug streams) through Ethernet-over-EtherCAT (EoE) or bulk CAN FD payloads, they risk overflowing communication channels and starving safety-critical control loops\index{Fieldbus!contention}.

On CAN FD networks, message arbitration is non-preemptive: once a low-priority diagnostic frame begins transmission on the physical layer, a newly ready high-priority emergency-stop or torque-command frame cannot preempt it. The resulting blocking latency depends on frame length, arbitration and data bit rates, and bit stuffing. Unregulated diagnostic bursts therefore inflate queueing jitter and exhaust hard timing budgets, even though every frame on the bus is structurally valid. Because CAN controllers do not register arbitration delays or link saturation as electrical errors, hardware error counters remain clean while safety deadlines expire. Similarly, while an EtherCAT master partitions cyclic process data from acyclic mailbox traffic, shared host network interface cards, protocol stack buffers, and slave microcontroller processing pipelines can still experience severe resource contention under heavy mailbox load. If mailbox servicing delays PDO packet processing or causes host-side scheduling jitter, safety heartbeats fail.

When unbudgeted telemetry delays a safety lease renewal or drive update past its deadline, the affected watchdog must invoke its qualified local fail-safe response. Furthermore, if a physical emergency-stop command travels across that same saturated bus, transmission delays directly consume stopping clearance. Verification trials must capture synchronized electrical communication traces alongside physical vehicle trajectories; observing a software timeout in isolation cannot prove that the machine arrested motion within its certified clearance envelope.

**Unbudgeted diagnostic traffic can delay the commands and evidence needed for a bounded response.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Physically isolate high-bandwidth diagnostic telemetry from real-time safety buses on separate network media, or enforce rigorous protocol-specific traffic shaping: strict frame-length caps, reserved identifier priorities, and rate-limiting ingress filters on CAN FD; dedicated cyclic and mailbox schedule partitioning with strict execution time budgets on EtherCAT. Ethernet Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) scheduling and frame preemption standards (IEEE 802.1Qbv and 802.1Qbu) apply only to compliant Ethernet hardware; they do not provide preemption across CAN FD or standard EtherCAT links.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying on software anomaly detectors that share electrical power or failure modes with monitored actuators.*

Actuator dynamics, including rapid motor acceleration, locked-rotor stall currents, and sharp regenerative braking transitions, cause severe electrical disturbances on shared power rails and analog ground references. Inverter switching produces steep inductive voltage transients ($\InductiveVoltage = \PowerRailInductance\,d\ConductorCurrent/d\TimeInstant$), while wiring harnesses and internal battery impedance introduce substantial voltage drops that can pull unregulated bus voltages below the minimum dropout threshold of downstream DC-DC converters. Adversarial testing campaigns (such as fault category F4) inject calibrated rail transients to measure whether these disturbances propagate into supposedly isolated sensor and safety controller supplies.

When digital transducers monitoring actuator velocity or position share a power distribution board, ground plane, or non-isolated buck regulator with motor gate drivers, supply dips and ground bounce propagate directly into sensor microcontrollers. A common failure mode is a frozen peripheral register: the transducer continues transmitting cyclically valid bus frames whose measurement payload has stopped updating. System behavior depends critically on representation: if an encoder freezes its cumulative position counter, a downstream velocity estimator that computes numerical derivatives will incorrectly deduce that the motor has reached zero velocity. Conversely, if the sensor freezes an internally computed velocity register, it may continuously report a nominal cruising speed.

For example, if a frozen velocity register continues reporting `{python} RackEndVerification.v_aisle_str` while the motor drive erroneously executes a full-throttle acceleration command, the telemetry frames will exhibit valid cyclic checksums and plausible values despite being physically decoupled from reality. A software anomaly detector that monitors only motor telemetry cannot identify the divergence without an independent physical motion witness, such as a secondary wheel encoder, an inertial measurement unit, or optical flow sensors. The adversarial verification suite must explicitly inject both the electrical transient and the resulting register freeze, using external ground-truth tracking to monitor vehicle kinematics through the commanded stop.

**A power fault that disrupts an actuator can simultaneously blind the sensor tasked with detecting it.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Power safety-critical transducers and monitor microcontrollers from galvanically isolated, held-up auxiliary supplies equipped with sufficient energy-storage capacitance to ride through worst-case bus transients. Transducers must be configured so that internal hardware faults cannot masquerade as plausible measurements. For analog transducers, pulling an output to 0 V fails this requirement whenever 0 V represents a valid physical reading (such as zero speed or minimum distance); reliable systems employ a "live zero" architecture with out-of-band diagnostic voltage levels, patterned after the NAMUR NE 43 standard for industrial transmitters [@namurne43]. For digital fieldbuses, enforce end-to-end communication protections featuring monotonic rolling sequence counters, timestamp freshness checks, and payload CRCs to detect repeated or corrupted frames [@autosare2e]. A frozen measurement register can still travel in a fresh, correctly sequenced packet, so detecting that failure also requires monitoring physical acquisition progress and cross-checking the reported state against an independent motion witness.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Treating an unobservable test outcome where diagnostic loggers dropped packets as evidence of safety.*

High-severity fault injection, such as short-circuiting an inverter drive phase, opening a contactor under full load, or coupling high-voltage electromagnetic interference (EMI) onto fieldbus cabling, generates intense radiated and conducted electrical transients within the test cell. Ground bounce and high inductive kickback routinely couple into the external data acquisition (DAQ) harness, desynchronizing high-speed digitizer clocks, overflowing PCIe frame-grabber ring buffers, or crashing host logging daemons into kernel panics.

Meanwhile, the physical mobile base comes to rest: either its spring-applied mechanical brakes engaged, its drive back-drove the gearbox to a stall, or it drifted into the test cell's mechanical end-stop buffer. In an undisciplined test campaign, observers look at the stopped machine and declare the run a "PASS" ("no crash occurred and the system reached rest"), while dismissing the missing telemetry as an irrelevant "instrumentation glitch" or repeating the trial until the logger manages to survive.

This practice introduces **survivorship bias**\index{Survivorship bias!verification}. The trials in which the logger crashes are often those with the most violent electrical transients, which are the conditions most likely to cause the safety microcontroller to hang in an exception handler without commanding deceleration. An unrecorded trial cannot reveal which mechanism stopped the base, and an operational warehouse aisle has no end-stop buffer. Under a rigorous qualification methodology, any test run lacking continuous, verifiable telemetry must be classified as `UNOBSERVABLE` and treated as an immediate test defect. The campaign must report the explicit count of each verdict alongside all untested configurations. Summary ratios such as $\PassedTrialCount / \TotalExecutedTrialCount$ serve as test-suite execution statistics rather than empirical failure-probability estimates derived from valid, independently scored trials. Before repeating that condition, the team must establish why the witnesses failed and qualify evidence capture under the injected environment.

**Discarding unobservable trials conceals the exact vulnerability under test through survivorship bias.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Categorize any test run with dropped, incomplete, or corrupted evidence as `UNOBSERVABLE`, retaining it as an evidence deficit whose cause must be investigated. Report all four verdict counts. Credit a required trial toward a protective claim only when its required evidence is complete and verified; repeated observable runs do not erase missing evidence from prior trials.

:::

## Summary {#sec-verification-summary}

The rack-end stopping claim begins as a physical distance and timing budget. Adversarial verification transforms this kinematic budget into a concrete, testable engineering contract by declaring the operating envelope across which it must hold, including the coupled corners that one-variable-at-a-time sweeps miss. A five-part test contract (bounded claim, declared conditions, precommitted oracle, stated injection procedure, provenance) decides whether any trial counts as evidence, and within it each postulated fault is built from a five-element chain: the negated nominal condition, the injection point, the expected detector, the bounded physical response, and an observable pass condition scored on an independent witness. For example, when the chunk policy stalls while its host processor continues transmitting nominal heartbeats, the verification harness evaluates powered deceleration onset and travel to rest referenced strictly from the timestamp of the last valid lease renewal. An automated oracle configured prior to the trial classifies each run into one of four mutually exclusive outcomes: `PASS`, `FAIL`, `INVALID`, or `UNOBSERVABLE`. Test coverage is then reported dimension by dimension, and the campaign is judged by its weakest dimension rather than by one aggregate percentage.

Developing a comprehensive fault catalog requires combining multiple analytical perspectives: inverting nominal design assumptions, tracing causal failure paths forward through physical mechanisms, evaluating authority boundaries, identifying shared root causes that induce coupled failures, and modeling adversarial disturbances at physical transducers. Some failure modes bypass communication buses and hardware sensors entirely. An adversarial physical patch, an optical spoof, or a maliciously crafted task instruction steers the learned proposer directly, testing the boundary of the proposal subsystem. Because the deterministic permission path monitors physical safety invariants rather than the semantic origin of a proposal, it intervenes only when an actuator command threatens a measured envelope limit. Consequently, such trials score strictly against the physical oracle. If an adversarial proposal induces an erratic or sub-optimal action that nonetheless remains entirely within the safe physical envelope, the physical predicates may pass, while the verification harness records the wrong action as a task-level coverage deficit rather than crediting it as a passed proposer-injection case.

Verification evidence must be gathered on the qualification rung that faithfully models the underlying physical mechanism. A software simulation cannot sag a power rail it does not model, whereas formal methods can verify compact, deterministic safety filters under explicit premises without establishing a closed-loop guarantee for the running machine's learned proposers. On physical test benches, hardware fault injectors operate directly at interface boundaries, while instrumentation towers record ground truth using independent clocks and isolated power supplies to prevent observer coupling. During falsification, Signal Temporal Logic provides signed robustness margins that direct search algorithms toward worst-case counterexamples. However, simulated margins cannot transfer directly to physical claims without applying a discrepancy bound justified over the claimed conditions. Similarly, importance sampling converts targeted failure searches into operational failure rates only when the sampling proposal distribution is explicitly declared, covers the entire failure domain, and applies proper likelihood weights. In rare-event analysis, extreme value models support safety claims only to the extent justified by their distributional assumptions. A counterexample refutes a safety claim, whereas the absence of one leaves the unsearched domain open rather than certified.

Eight relations formalize this quantitative framework, and @tbl-15-key-equations summarizes what each bounds or decides.

| Equation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                                                                               | Derived                                                                     |
|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| $\HazardOnset \le \ChunkLease + \PermissionLoopPeriod + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime$, and $\StallTravelBound(\SpeedAtDetection) = \SpeedAtDetection\,(\ChunkLease + \PermissionLoopPeriod + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime) + \ResidentStopDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) + \TrackingErrorBound$ | F1's two precommitted predicates, measured from the last valid renewal; the capture-referenced budget subtotal cannot stand in for them                                                 | @eq-verification-f1-oracle                                                  |
| $\UnmitigatedHardwareFaultRate = \RawHardwareFaultRate(1 - \DiagnosticCoverage)$, $\;\ZeroFailureTrialCount \ge \ln(1-\ConfidenceLevel)/\ln \DiagnosticCoverage$                                                                                                                                                               | The diagnostic coverage a rate target demands, and the zero-miss injections, sampled in proportion to the fault rates, that demonstrate it                                              | Notebook \ref{nbk-verification-hardware-fault-injection-coverage-mean-time} |
| $\BlackoutClockConversionError = \ClockSynchronizationSkew\,\SynchronizationBlackout + \TimingJitter$                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | How much of the clock-conversion bound behind F2's refusal threshold a synchronization blackout spends                                                                                  | @eq-verification-clock-drift                                                |
| $\StlRobustness(\square_{[0,\FiniteTimeHorizon]}\StlFormula) = \min_t \StlRobustness(\StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory, \TimeInstant)$, $\;\StlRobustness(\lozenge_{[0,\StlEventuallyDeadline]}\StlFormula) = \max_t \StlRobustness(\StlFormula, \SignalTrajectory, \TimeInstant)$                                                | The signed margin of a trace against a temporal requirement, the score a falsifier drives toward zero                                                                                   | @eq-verification-stl-recursive-robustness                                   |

| $\SimulatedReturnLevel + \PredicateLipschitzConstant\,\TransferDiscrepancyBound \le \ClearDistance - \KnownComponentStopDistance$                                                                                                                                                                                              | Whether a discounted tail estimate fits inside the physical reserve; a necessary check, not a release rule                                                                              | @eq-verification-evt-release-condition                                      |

: **Key equations of adversarial verification**: The relations that turn a stopping budget into precommitted predicates, size a fault-injection campaign, and limit what search, simulation, and rare-event statistics can claim, with the place each is derived. {#tbl-15-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[40,42,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Adversarial verification and fault injection"}
* **A fault tests a physical claim:** Derive the injection, detector, response, and independent witness from the stopping or contact bound. Successful task execution alone does not exercise the protective response.
* **The environment bounds the evidence:** Select each qualification rung for the mechanism it exercises. Simulation, processor execution, electrical benches, and physical rigs contribute complementary evidence with different blind spots.
* **Search finds counterexamples, not universal passes:** Signed temporal margins help prioritize disturbances near a violation. An unsuccessful search does not establish a global minimum, and a fitted tail does not prove a hard physical limit.
* **Precommitment preserves the meaning of a pass:** Fix conditions and predicates before injection. Keep `FAIL`, `INVALID`, and `UNOBSERVABLE` distinct, because missing or invalid evidence cannot support the stopping claim.
* **Verification hands release bounded evidence:** Bind each fault record to its claim, builds, conditions, and raw measurements. Coverage gaps and model assumptions remain part of the fault records, so release can restrict authority where evidence ends.

:::

Adversarial verification is where the fourth law, evidence bounds authority (principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority}), acquires its evidence. Each fault record names the claim it supports, the envelope point it covered, and the oracle fixed before the run, so the authority that the release decision can grant reaches exactly as far as the passing records and stops at every `INVALID`, `UNOBSERVABLE`, or untested cell. The F1 record of this chapter shows the rule in its plainest form. Its timing path, candidate envelope point, and witnesses are specified, while its loaded braking premise remains unqualified and its outcome field is empty, and until measured trials on a physical rig with independent instrumentation fill that field, the stopping claim it describes grants no authority at all.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-verification-history}

Deliberate fault injection originated in the dependability community of the 1980s, where researchers applied electrical transients, pin-level shorts, and radiation directly to working microprocessors to determine whether fault-tolerant architectures could detect and contain hardware errors. @arlat1990fault formalized this methodology with the MESSALINE tool, structuring each verification campaign around four operational dimensions: the injected faults, the workload activating them, the readouts captured across system boundaries, and the dependability measures derived from observations. This four-part taxonomy serves as the foundational template for the fault records developed throughout this chapter. As systems scaled in complexity, fault injection transitioned from physical pin manipulation to software instrumentation. The comprehensive survey by @hsueh1997fault framed the defining engineering trade-off: hardware-implemented injection manipulates internal signals and electrical states unreachable by software, whereas software-implemented injection offers programmatic repeatability and lower operational cost at the expense of ignoring low-level hardware faults. This trade-off reappears at every rung of the cyber-physical qualification ladder. Early practitioners also discovered that monitoring hooks and profiling code unavoidably perturb execution timing and cache states, a distortion @gait1986probe termed the *probe effect*. Because sub-millisecond timing shifts can destabilize physical feedback loops, high-assurance verification architectures isolate witness observers onto independent power supplies and dedicated clock domains.

Search-based falsification and continuous verification followed a parallel lineage rooted in formal methods and statistical physics. @pnueli1977temporal first introduced linear temporal logic to prove correctness properties over discrete program executions. To verify continuous and hybrid physical trajectories, @maler2004monitoring generalized temporal assertions into signal temporal logic (STL). @fainekos2009robustness subsequently equipped STL with quantitative spatial semantics, replacing binary true-false verdicts with a continuous signed distance margin. This formulation transformed the falsification problem from an intractable combinatorial search into continuous gradient-free or gradient-based optimization. Cyber-physical falsification frameworks such as S-TaLiRo [@annpureddy2011staliro] and Breach [@donze2010breach] packaged these continuous margins to automate the discovery of safety violations in nonlinear dynamical models. Statistical rare-event estimation has an even older heritage. Importance sampling emerged from early Monte Carlo radiation shielding calculations by @kahn1953methods, the cross-entropy method introduced adaptive proposal distributions [@rubinstein2004cross], and @okelly2018scalable synthesized both techniques to quantify catastrophic collision probabilities across autonomous driving stacks. When safety analysts must characterize worst-case physical excursions without imposing restrictive global distribution assumptions, they draw on extreme value theory, which entered engineering through the flood-frequency analyses of @gumbel1958statistics and was rigorously established in its modern peaks-over-threshold form by @balkema1974residual and @pickands1975statistical.

Formal verification of learned neural controllers is the most recent strand. Reluplex [@katz2017reluplex] proved that modified simplex constraint solvers could formally verify input-output safety properties on small piecewise-linear networks. Subsequent bound-propagation frameworks, including α,β-CROWN [@wang2021betacrown], scaled formal guarantees to million-parameter vision networks using branch-and-bound techniques and convex relaxation. However, formal solvers remain computationally bounded; the cited results do not establish guarantees for multi-billion-parameter vision-language-action foundation models operating in closed feedback loops. The verification architecture developed in this chapter unifies these historical lineages into a cohesive systems discipline. Each trial executes against an explicit operational claim, evaluates trajectories with an oracle declared prior to the run, isolates observational telemetry within uncorrupted witness hardware, and exports fault records that carry measured coverage deficits into deployment safety cases.

Six foundational works trace the trajectory from classical hardware dependability to modern cyber-physical validation algorithms:

- @arlat1990fault establishes fault injection as a controlled experimental science, defining the four-factor schema of faults, activation workloads, readouts, and derived measures that governs the fault records in @sec-verification-manifest-coverage.
- @leveson2011engineering introduces Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) and System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA), establishing the forward hazard methodology in @sec-verification-forward-analysis that identifies systemic safety violations emerging from unsafe control interactions rather than isolated component failures.
- @fainekos2009robustness formulates the continuous spatial robustness degree for temporal logic specifications over real-valued signals, providing the signed optimization margin evaluated throughout @sec-verification-stl-robustness.
- @owen2013monte provides a definitive mathematical foundation for importance sampling and rare-event estimation, detailing effective sample size diagnostics, weight degeneracies, and failure modes where unrepresentative proposals yield falsely optimistic variance estimates.
- @corso2021survey surveys algorithmic safety validation for black-box autonomous systems, categorizing falsification approaches according to whether they target counterexample discovery, most-likely-failure trajectories, or rare failure probabilities.
- @kochenderfer2026validation synthesizes trajectory falsification, failure-probability estimation, reachable set analysis, and runtime monitoring into an algorithmic discipline for validating complex autonomous systems.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From verification to release decisions"}
Verification delivers to the release gate a signed set of fault records, the per-rung coverage of the qualification ladder behind them, and an explicit account of the operating regimes no trial reached. For each safety claim, the set binds the corresponding fault records to any sim-to-real transfer bound ($\TransferDiscrepancyBound$) or rare-event tail estimate on which the claim depends, keeping measured margins, conditional model estimates, and untested regimes strictly apart. Verification records supply behavioral evidence under fault conditions, but they do not make deployment policy, and no individual fault record decides whether the machine may operate in production aisles. In @sec-release, the release process writes each claim as a physical inequality, joins these fault records with the authority record, the placement record, and the evaluation record in a safety case, and judges which claims are substantiated, which release verdict applies (`UNCOND`, `COND`, or `REFUSE`), and which standing conditions must govern live operation.
:::
